summary: The smallest thing Kubernetes can run: one or more containers that share a network address and storage.
explanation:
A Pod is a wrapper around one or more containers that are guaranteed to run on the same node, at the same time, sharing the same network namespace and the same set of volumes. Because they share a network namespace, containers in a Pod reach each other on `localhost` and cannot both bind the same port. That shared-fate bundle is the unit Kubernetes schedules — the scheduler never places half a Pod.

Every Pod gets its own cluster-internal IP address. Containers inside it are not individually addressable; traffic arrives at the Pod IP and a port. When the Pod dies, that IP is gone forever — a replacement Pod gets a new one. This is exactly why Services exist: you need a stable name in front of an unstable set of Pod IPs.

Pods are deliberately fragile. Nothing restarts a Pod that you created directly if its node reboots or is drained — the Pod object simply ends up in a terminal phase and stays there. Controllers such as Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets exist to create replacement Pods for you. In practice you almost never write a bare Pod outside of debugging.

Most Pod fields are immutable once created. You can change the container image, `activeDeadlineSeconds`, tolerations and a few others; you cannot change the command, the labels' role in a selector, or most of the spec. To "edit" a Pod, you replace it — which is what a rolling update actually does.
whenToUse: One-off debugging: run a shell in the cluster to test DNS or connectivity
Learning — to see the object every other workload controller eventually produces
Sidecar patterns where two processes genuinely must share a network namespace and disk
Almost never in production directly; use a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job

keyFields.description: The list of containers to run. At least one is required, and each needs a name and an image.
What the scheduler reserves on a node when placing the Pod. Requests, not limits, drive scheduling.
The hard ceiling enforced at runtime. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed; exceeding CPU just throttles it.
Always (default), OnFailure or Never. Applies to containers within the Pod, not to recreating the Pod itself.
Containers that run to completion, one at a time, before the main containers start. Used for setup and waiting on dependencies.
Simple key/value constraint on which nodes are eligible.
Storage made available to the Pod, mounted into containers via volumeMounts.
Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed or Unknown. Coarse-grained; container statuses carry the real detail.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: debug-shell
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: debug-shell
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: shell
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 10m
          memory: 32Mi
        limits:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 64Mi
      volumeMounts:
        - name: scratch
          mountPath: /scratch
  volumes:
    - name: scratch
      emptyDir: {}
commonMistakes: Creating bare Pods in production. Nothing recreates them — drain the node and the workload is simply gone.
Setting a memory limit far above the request. The Pod schedules onto a node that cannot actually satisfy the limit, and gets OOM-killed under load.
Assuming the Pod IP is stable. It changes on every restart; anything that hardcodes it breaks.
Putting unrelated containers in one Pod because 'they go together'. They then scale together, restart together, and fight over the same port space.
kubectlTips: kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh  — throwaway debug Pod that deletes itself on exit
kubectl describe pod <name>  — the Events section at the bottom is where scheduling and image-pull failures are explained
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous  — logs from the crashed instance, not the current one
kubectl get pod <name> -o wide  — shows the node and Pod IP

summary: Keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running, recreating them whenever one disappears.
explanation:
A ReplicaSet runs one simple loop: count the Pods matching my selector, compare to `spec.replicas`, then create or delete Pods to close the gap. That is the whole job. It has no concept of versions, rollouts, or history.

The link between a ReplicaSet and its Pods is `spec.selector`, a label query. The ReplicaSet also stamps `metadata.ownerReferences` onto Pods it creates, which is what lets garbage collection delete the Pods when the ReplicaSet is deleted. But adoption works purely by labels: if a bare Pod already carries matching labels, the ReplicaSet will adopt it and count it toward the replica total rather than creating a new one.

You rarely create ReplicaSets yourself. A Deployment creates them for you — one per template revision — and scales them up and down to perform rollouts. Understanding this is the key to understanding Deployments: the Deployment does not manage Pods, it manages ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet manages Pods.

`spec.selector` is immutable after creation. If you need a different selector, you delete and recreate the object.
whenToUse: Almost never directly — use a Deployment, which manages ReplicaSets for you
When you want replica-keeping with absolutely no rollout machinery
Reading one to understand what a Deployment actually did during a rollout

keyFields.description: Desired number of matching Pods. Defaults to 1 if omitted.
Label query identifying which Pods this ReplicaSet owns. Immutable, and must match spec.template.metadata.labels.
The Pod template used to create new Pods. Editing it does NOT restart existing Pods — only newly created ones use it.
How many owned Pods are passing their readiness checks, as opposed to merely existing.

example:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
commonMistakes: Editing the Pod template on a ReplicaSet and expecting a rolling update. Nothing happens to running Pods; only replacements pick up the change.
Making spec.selector not match spec.template.metadata.labels. The API server rejects this outright.
Using a selector so broad it adopts unrelated Pods, which then get deleted when the ReplicaSet scales down.
Creating a ReplicaSet when a Deployment was wanted, then discovering there is no rollback and no rollout history.
kubectlTips: kubectl get rs  — during a Deployment rollout you will see the old and new ReplicaSets side by side
kubectl get rs -o wide  — shows the container images, which is how you tell revisions apart
kubectl describe rs <name>  — Events show Pod create and delete decisions

summary: Runs a stateless application and updates it gradually, with the ability to roll back to a previous version.
explanation:
A Deployment does not create Pods. It creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet creates the Pods. That indirection is the entire point: it is what makes rollbacks possible.

When you change the Pod template, the Deployment controller hashes the new template and creates a brand-new ReplicaSet for it, then shifts replicas from the old ReplicaSet to the new one a few at a time. `maxUnavailable` caps how far below the desired count you may dip; `maxSurge` caps how far above it you may temporarily go. The old ReplicaSet is scaled to zero but kept, up to `revisionHistoryLimit`. A rollback is therefore not a redeploy — it is just scaling an old ReplicaSet back up.

A rollout only progresses when new Pods become Ready. If your readiness probe never passes, the rollout stalls rather than replacing healthy Pods with broken ones — which is the safety property you are paying for. After `progressDeadlineSeconds` with no progress, the Deployment is marked as failed in its conditions, though it does not automatically roll back.

Deployments assume Pods are interchangeable: any replica can serve any request, and they can start and stop in any order. If replicas need stable identities, stable storage, or ordered startup, you want a StatefulSet instead.
whenToUse: Stateless HTTP services and APIs — the default choice for most workloads
Anything where replicas are interchangeable and can restart in any order
When you need gradual rollouts and one-command rollback
Workloads that should scale horizontally, often driven by an HPA

keyFields.description: Desired Pod count. Omit it if an HPA manages scaling, so the two do not fight.
Label query for owned Pods. Immutable after creation.
Pod template. Any change here triggers a new ReplicaSet and a rollout.
RollingUpdate (default) or Recreate. Recreate kills every old Pod before starting new ones, causing downtime.
How many Pods may be unavailable during the rollout. Count or percentage; default 25%.
How many extra Pods may exist above spec.replicas during the rollout. Default 25%.
How many old ReplicaSets to retain for rollback. Default 10.
Seconds of no rollout progress before the Deployment is marked failed. Default 600.
How long a new Pod must be Ready before it counts as available, guarding against Pods that crash a second after starting.

example:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 3
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: http
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
commonMistakes: No readiness probe. Kubernetes then treats a Pod as ready the moment the process starts, so a rollout can route traffic to an app that is still booting.
Using image tag :latest. Two Pods created minutes apart can run different code, and rolling back changes nothing because the tag is the same.
Setting spec.replicas in Git while an HPA also manages it. Every reconcile fights the autoscaler and replicas oscillate.
Expecting a Deployment to give stable Pod names or per-replica storage. It will not — that is a StatefulSet.
Assuming a rollback re-pulls old images. It scales up the old ReplicaSet, so if that image tag was overwritten in the registry you get the new code back.
kubectlTips: kubectl rollout status deploy/web  — watch a rollout finish; exits non-zero if it fails, which makes it useful in CI
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web  — roll back to the previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web --to-revision=3  — roll back to a specific revision
kubectl rollout history deploy/web  — list revisions
kubectl rollout restart deploy/web  — restart all Pods by stamping a new annotation on the template
kubectl set image deploy/web nginx=nginx:1.27.1  — trigger a rollout without editing YAML

summary: Runs Pods that each need a stable name, a stable network identity, and their own persistent disk.
explanation:
A StatefulSet gives each replica a durable identity. Pods are named `<statefulset>-0`, `<statefulset>-1`, and so on, and those names are reused: if `web-1` is deleted, its replacement is also called `web-1`, gets the same DNS name, and reattaches the same volume. A Deployment gives you random suffixes and fresh storage; a StatefulSet gives you the opposite.

Storage comes from `volumeClaimTemplates`. The controller creates one PersistentVolumeClaim per replica, named `<template>-<statefulset>-<ordinal>`, and those PVCs deliberately outlive the Pods — and, by default, outlive the StatefulSet itself. Deleting the StatefulSet does not delete the data unless you also delete the PVCs, or set `persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy`.

Stable DNS requires a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) named in `spec.serviceName`. With it, each Pod is resolvable at `<pod-name>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. This is how a database cluster member advertises itself to its peers, and it is why the headless Service is not optional.

By default operations are ordered and sequential: Pod N is not created until Pod N-1 is Running and Ready, and scale-down happens in reverse ordinal order. Updates roll from the highest ordinal downward, and `spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition` lets you hold the rollout at a given ordinal for a staged canary.
whenToUse: Databases and datastores: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Cassandra
Quorum systems that need stable peer addresses: etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka
Any workload where replica 0 and replica 1 are meaningfully different
When each replica needs its own PersistentVolume that survives rescheduling

keyFields.description: Name of the headless Service that provides per-Pod DNS. Required for stable network identity.
PVC templates; one PVC is created per replica and follows that ordinal for life.
OrderedReady (default, one at a time) or Parallel (all at once). Immutable after creation.
RollingUpdate (default) or OnDelete, where you delete Pods yourself to trigger updates.
Only Pods with ordinal >= this value are updated. The staged-canary control.
Whether generated PVCs are deleted when the StatefulSet is deleted or scaled down. Defaults to Retain for both.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: postgres
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
    - name: postgres
      port: 5432
      targetPort: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          ports:
            - name: postgres
              containerPort: 5432
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: postgres-secret
                  key: password
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 512Mi
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: standard
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi
commonMistakes: Forgetting the headless Service, or pointing spec.serviceName at a normal ClusterIP Service. Per-Pod DNS never resolves and peers cannot find each other.
Expecting `kubectl delete sts` to clean up storage. The PVCs remain by default, and so does the cloud disk bill.
Trying to grow a volumeClaimTemplate by editing it. The field is immutable; you must resize the individual PVCs instead.
Assuming a StatefulSet makes an application clustered. It provides identity and storage only — replication and leader election are the application's job.
A single failing Pod blocks the whole rollout under the default OrderedReady policy, because ordinal N-1 must be Ready first.
kubectlTips: kubectl get pvc -l app=postgres  — see the per-replica claims the StatefulSet created
kubectl delete sts postgres --cascade=orphan  — remove the controller but leave the Pods running
kubectl exec postgres-0 -- nslookup postgres-1.postgres  — verify per-Pod DNS works
kubectl rollout status sts/postgres  — track an ordered update

summary: Runs exactly one copy of a Pod on every node (or every node matching a selector).
explanation:
A DaemonSet has no `replicas` field, because the replica count is decided by the cluster, not by you: it is the number of eligible nodes. The controller watches the Node list and creates one Pod per node. Add a node and a Pod appears on it automatically; remove a node and its Pod goes away with it.

This is the shape you want for per-node infrastructure — log collectors, metrics agents, CNI plugins, CSI node drivers, security agents. These need to see the node itself, so DaemonSet Pods commonly mount host paths, use `hostNetwork: true`, or run privileged, all of which are unusual and deserve scrutiny in ordinary application Pods.

Eligibility is controlled by `spec.template.spec.nodeSelector` or `affinity`, and by tolerations. Control-plane nodes normally carry a taint such as `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`, so a DaemonSet only lands there if it tolerates that taint. Cluster-wide agents usually add broad tolerations on purpose; application-adjacent DaemonSets usually should not.

Updates use `spec.updateStrategy`. `RollingUpdate` (the default) replaces Pods node by node with `maxUnavailable` controlling how many nodes lose the agent at once; `OnDelete` updates a node's Pod only when you delete it manually.
whenToUse: Log shipping agents such as Fluent Bit or Vector
Node metrics exporters such as node-exporter
CNI network plugins and CSI node drivers
Security or compliance agents that must observe every node
Anything where 'one per node' is the correct count, not 'N total'

keyFields.description: Label query for owned Pods. Required and immutable.
Pod template placed on each eligible node.
Which node taints to tolerate. Without matching tolerations the DaemonSet skips tainted nodes such as control-plane nodes.
Restricts the DaemonSet to a subset of nodes, e.g. only GPU nodes.
RollingUpdate (default) or OnDelete.
How many nodes may be without the Pod at once during an update. Default 1.
Nodes where the daemon Pod is running and ready — compare against desiredNumberScheduled.

example:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-exporter
  namespace: monitoring
  labels:
    app: node-exporter
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: node-exporter
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: node-exporter
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true
      hostPID: true
      tolerations:
        - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: node-exporter
          image: quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.8.2
          args:
            - --path.rootfs=/host
          ports:
            - name: metrics
              containerPort: 9100
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: rootfs
              mountPath: /host
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: rootfs
          hostPath:
            path: /
            type: Directory
commonMistakes: Adding a replicas field. It does not exist on a DaemonSet and the API server rejects the manifest.
Forgetting tolerations and then wondering why control-plane nodes have no log agent.
Using hostPath mounts casually. It couples the Pod to the node's filesystem layout and is a common privilege-escalation path.
Requesting large CPU or memory. The request is multiplied by every node in the cluster, which can be hundreds of times more than expected.
Using hostNetwork with a fixed containerPort that another DaemonSet already binds — the second one stays Pending forever.
kubectlTips: kubectl get ds -A  — desired vs current vs ready across all namespaces, the fastest health check
kubectl rollout status ds/node-exporter -n monitoring  — track a node-by-node update
kubectl get pods -l app=node-exporter -o wide  — confirm one Pod per node and spot the node that is missing one

summary: Runs Pods until a set number of them finish successfully, then stops.
explanation:
A Job runs work that ends. It creates Pods and watches their exit codes: a container exiting 0 means success, anything else means failure. The Job is complete once `spec.completions` Pods have succeeded, and it will keep creating replacement Pods until then, up to `spec.backoffLimit` failures (default 6, with exponential backoff between retries).

The Pod template must set `restartPolicy` to `OnFailure` or `Never` — `Always` is rejected, because a Pod that always restarts can never complete. The choice matters: `OnFailure` restarts the container in place, keeping the same Pod, while `Never` leaves the failed Pod around and creates a new one, which is better for post-mortem debugging.

For parallel work, `spec.parallelism` sets how many Pods run at once and `spec.completions` how many successes are needed in total. Setting `completionMode: Indexed` gives each Pod a fixed index in the `batch.kubernetes.io/job-completion-index` annotation and in the `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` environment variable, so each worker can deterministically pick its own shard of the input.

Finished Jobs and their Pods stay around so you can read the logs. That is useful and also a slow leak — set `spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` and the TTL controller deletes the Job (and its Pods) automatically some seconds after it finishes.
whenToUse: Database schema migrations before a release
Batch data processing, imports and exports
One-off maintenance and backfill tasks
Fan-out work split across many parallel workers with Indexed completion

keyFields.description: How many Pods must succeed for the Job to be complete. Default 1.
How many Pods may run concurrently. Default 1.
How many failures to tolerate before marking the Job Failed. Default 6.
Wall-clock limit for the whole Job. Exceeding it terminates running Pods and fails the Job, overriding backoffLimit.
Seconds after completion before the Job and its Pods are garbage collected.
NonIndexed (default) or Indexed, which gives each Pod a stable completion index.
Must be OnFailure or Never. Always is invalid for a Job.
Rules to fail fast or ignore specific container exit codes rather than blindly retrying.

example:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
  namespace: default
spec:
  completions: 1
  parallelism: 1
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db-migrate
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: migrate/migrate:v4.17.1
          args:
            - -path=/migrations
            - -database=$(DATABASE_URL)
            - up
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-credentials
                  key: url
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
commonMistakes: Setting restartPolicy: Always in the Pod template. The API server rejects the Job outright.
Assuming a Job runs exactly once. Node failure or eviction can produce a second execution, so the work must be idempotent.
Forgetting ttlSecondsAfterFinished, leaving thousands of completed Pods consuming etcd space and cluttering kubectl output.
Editing a Job's template to re-run it. Most of a Job spec is immutable; delete and recreate it instead.
Relying on backoffLimit alone for a hung Job. A Pod that never exits is never a failure — you need activeDeadlineSeconds.
kubectlTips: kubectl logs job/db-migrate  — logs from a Pod belonging to the Job, without looking up the Pod name
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/db-migrate --timeout=300s  — block in CI until it finishes
kubectl get job db-migrate -o jsonpath='{.status.succeeded}'  — machine-readable success count
kubectl delete job db-migrate  — also deletes its Pods via owner references

summary: Creates a Job on a repeating schedule, written in standard cron syntax.
explanation:
A CronJob is a thin scheduler on top of Jobs. At each scheduled time it creates a new Job object from `spec.jobTemplate`, and that Job creates the Pods. So a CronJob produces Jobs, and Jobs produce Pods — three layers, which is why debugging means looking at all three.

The schedule uses the five-field cron format and is interpreted in UTC unless you set `spec.timeZone` to an IANA name such as `America/New_York`. Getting this wrong is the single most common CronJob bug: a job scheduled for `0 2 * * *` runs at 2am UTC, which may be the middle of the afternoon locally.

`spec.concurrencyPolicy` decides what happens when the previous run is still going. `Allow` (the default) lets runs overlap, `Forbid` skips the new run, and `Replace` kills the old one and starts fresh. For anything touching shared state, the default is usually wrong.

If the controller is down or the cluster is busy, a scheduled run can be missed. `startingDeadlineSeconds` says how late a run may still start; if more than 100 schedule times are missed without this field set, the controller gives up scheduling entirely and records an event — a surprising failure mode worth knowing about.
whenToUse: Nightly backups and database dumps
Periodic cleanup of stale records or temporary files
Scheduled report generation and data exports
Regular health or reconciliation sweeps

keyFields.description: Five-field cron expression, e.g. '0 3 * * *' for 03:00 daily.
IANA time zone name. Without it the schedule is UTC.
Allow (default), Forbid or Replace — how to handle a run that is still going when the next one is due.
Set true to stop creating new Jobs without deleting the CronJob.
How late a missed run may still start. Leaving it unset risks the 100-missed-schedules shutdown.
Completed Jobs to keep. Default 3.
Failed Jobs to keep. Default 1.
The Job spec used for each run — backoffLimit, parallelism and the Pod template all live here.

example:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule: "0 3 * * *"
  timeZone: "Etc/UTC"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 300
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: nightly-backup
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: postgres:16
              command:
                - /bin/sh
                - -c
                - pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" | gzip > /backup/dump-$(date +%F).sql.gz
              env:
                - name: DATABASE_URL
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: db-credentials
                      key: url
              volumeMounts:
                - name: backup
                  mountPath: /backup
              resources:
                requests:
                  cpu: 100m
                  memory: 256Mi
          volumes:
            - name: backup
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: backup-pvc
commonMistakes: Assuming the schedule uses local time. It is UTC unless spec.timeZone is set.
Leaving concurrencyPolicy at Allow for a job that is slower than its interval, so runs pile up and compete over the same data.
Quoting problems in the schedule: '0 3 * * *' must be quoted in YAML or the asterisks confuse the parser.
Expecting exactly-once semantics. CronJob is documented as at-least-once; a run can occasionally fire twice.
Not setting history limits, then finding hundreds of old Job objects still in the namespace.
kubectlTips: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/nightly-backup manual-run-1  — trigger a run right now to test it
kubectl patch cronjob nightly-backup -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'  — pause it without deleting it
kubectl get cronjob  — the LAST SCHEDULE column tells you whether it is actually firing
kubectl get jobs --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp  — see run history in order

summary: The original, now-superseded way to keep a set number of Pods running; use a Deployment instead.
explanation:
**Legacy.** ReplicationController is the first-generation replica keeper, from before `apps/v1` existed. It still works and has never been formally removed from the core `v1` API, but it has been effectively superseded since Kubernetes 1.2 and no new workload should use it.

Functionally it is a weaker ReplicaSet. Its selector is a flat map of exact label matches under `spec.selector`, with no `matchLabels`/`matchExpressions` structure, so it cannot express set-based queries like `env in (staging, prod)`. That limitation is the main reason ReplicaSet replaced it.

The modern equivalent is a Deployment, which manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods. You get rolling updates, revision history and rollback — none of which a ReplicationController has. The old `kubectl rolling-update` command that drove ReplicationController updates client-side was removed years ago.

It is worth recognising in old manifests and tutorials, and worth converting: the shape of the object is nearly identical, so migration is mostly changing `apiVersion` and `kind` and nesting the selector under `matchLabels`.
whenToUse: Reading or migrating very old manifests — that is genuinely the only reason
Never for new work; use a Deployment

keyFields.description: Desired Pod count. Default 1.
A flat map of exact label matches — no matchLabels or matchExpressions. If omitted it defaults to the template's labels.
Pod template used for new Pods. Changing it does not update existing Pods.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReplicationController
metadata:
  name: legacy-web
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    app: legacy-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: legacy-web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
commonMistakes: Choosing it for new workloads because an old tutorial used it — you silently give up rollouts and rollback.
Writing a matchLabels block under spec.selector. That structure belongs to ReplicaSet; here the selector is a flat map and the manifest will be rejected.
Looking for kubectl rolling-update to update it. That command no longer exists.
kubectlTips: kubectl get rc  — find any lingering ReplicationControllers in a cluster
kubectl get rc -A -o name  — audit every namespace for legacy objects worth migrating

summary: A stable name and IP address in front of a changing set of Pods, with traffic spread across them.
explanation:
Pod IPs are disposable — every restart produces a new one. A Service solves that by allocating one virtual IP (the ClusterIP) that never changes for the life of the Service, plus a DNS name `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`. Clients talk to the name; Kubernetes handles the moving parts behind it.

Membership is by label selector, not by a list of Pods. The endpoints controller continuously watches for Pods matching `spec.selector` and writes the ready ones into EndpointSlice objects. `kube-proxy` on each node turns those EndpointSlices into iptables or IPVS rules that rewrite the destination address of packets aimed at the ClusterIP. There is no proxy process in the data path and no single point of failure — just packet-rewriting rules on every node. Crucially, only Pods passing their readiness probe are included, which is how rolling updates avoid sending traffic to Pods that are still starting.

There are four types. **ClusterIP** (default) is reachable only inside the cluster. **NodePort** additionally opens the same port on every node (default range 30000-32767) and forwards it to the Service. **LoadBalancer** builds on NodePort and asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer; on a bare-metal cluster with no such controller, the external IP stays `<pending>` forever. **ExternalName** is different in kind: it creates no ClusterIP and no proxying at all, just a DNS CNAME to an external hostname.

Setting `clusterIP: None` makes a **headless** Service. No virtual IP is allocated and no proxying happens; DNS returns the Pod IPs directly, one A record per ready Pod. This is what StatefulSets use for per-Pod DNS, and what clients that do their own load balancing or connection pooling usually want.
whenToUse: ClusterIP: internal service-to-service traffic — the default and by far the most common
NodePort: quick external access in dev clusters, or as a backend for an external load balancer
LoadBalancer: exposing a single service to the internet on a cloud provider
ExternalName: giving an out-of-cluster hostname a stable in-cluster alias
Headless: StatefulSet peer discovery, or clients that need real Pod IPs

keyFields.description: Labels identifying backing Pods. Omit it to manage EndpointSlices manually.
ClusterIP (default), NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName.
The port the Service listens on.
The port on the Pod. Can be a number or a named container port; defaults to the value of port.
The port opened on every node, for NodePort and LoadBalancer types. Auto-assigned if omitted.
Set to None for a headless Service. Otherwise assigned automatically and immutable.
None (default) or ClientIP to pin a client to one Pod.
Cluster (default) or Local. Local preserves the client source IP but only routes to Pods on the receiving node.
SingleStack, PreferDualStack or RequireDualStack for IPv4/IPv6 clusters.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
    - name: metrics
      protocol: TCP
      port: 9090
      targetPort: 9090
commonMistakes: Selector labels that do not match the Pod labels. The Service is created happily, has zero endpoints, and every connection is refused.
Confusing port and targetPort. port is what clients dial; targetPort is what the container listens on.
Expecting a LoadBalancer to work on bare metal or in kind/minikube without MetalLB or an equivalent — the external IP stays pending.
Assuming a Service load-balances long-lived connections. It balances at connection time, so a persistent gRPC or HTTP/2 connection stays pinned to one Pod.
Pods with no readiness probe are treated as ready immediately, so the Service routes traffic to applications that have not finished starting.
kubectlTips: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web  — the real answer to 'why is my Service returning nothing'
kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80  — reach a ClusterIP Service from your laptop
kubectl expose deploy/web --port=80 --target-port=8080  — generate a Service from an existing Deployment
kubectl run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -s http://web.default.svc.cluster.local  — test resolution from inside the cluster

summary: HTTP routing rules that send requests for particular hostnames and paths to different Services.
explanation:
An Ingress is a set of layer-7 routing rules: for this hostname and this path prefix, send the request to that Service on that port. It also holds TLS configuration, pointing at Secrets that contain certificates.

An Ingress object on its own does nothing. It is data, not a running proxy. You must install an ingress controller — ingress-nginx, Traefik, HAProxy, or a cloud provider's — which watches Ingress objects and reconfigures a real proxy to match. A cluster with no controller will accept your Ingress and route nothing, which is the most common first-time surprise.

Which controller handles an Ingress is decided by `spec.ingressClassName`, referencing an IngressClass object. The old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation did the same job and is deprecated; use the field. If neither is set, the controller marked as cluster default picks it up.

`pathType` is required on every path and its meaning matters. `Prefix` matches on whole path segments, so `/api` matches `/api/v1` but not `/apiary`. `Exact` matches the entire path only. `ImplementationSpecific` hands interpretation to the controller, which is how regular expressions and rewrites happen — always via controller-specific annotations, since the Ingress spec itself covers only basic routing. That annotation dependence is the main reason the Gateway API was created.
whenToUse: Exposing several HTTP services through one external IP and one load balancer
Name-based virtual hosting — several hostnames on a single entry point
Terminating TLS in one place with certificates from cert-manager
Not for raw TCP or UDP; Ingress is HTTP/HTTPS only

keyFields.description: Which IngressClass, and therefore which controller, should implement these rules.
Hostname to match. Omit to match any host.
The URL path to match.
Prefix, Exact or ImplementationSpecific. Required — there is no default.
Target Service name and port. The Service must exist in the same namespace as the Ingress.
Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls holding the certificate and key, in the Ingress's namespace.
Where to send requests matching no rule.

example:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - shop.example.com
      secretName: shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api
                port:
                  number: 80
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web
                port:
                  name: http
commonMistakes: Expecting an Ingress to work with no ingress controller installed. Nothing routes and there is no error to see.
Omitting pathType. It is a required field in networking.k8s.io/v1 and the manifest is rejected.
Referencing a Service or TLS Secret in another namespace. Ingress backends and TLS Secrets must be in the Ingress's own namespace.
Copying extensions/v1beta1 examples from old blog posts. That API version was removed in Kubernetes 1.22.
Assuming Prefix matches substrings. It matches path segments, so /api does not match /apiary.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe ing web  — shows the rules the controller parsed and any errors it reported
kubectl get ing -A  — the ADDRESS column is empty until a controller assigns one
kubectl get ingressclass  — check which classes exist and which is the default

summary: Names an ingress controller so Ingress objects can say which one should handle them.
explanation:
When a cluster has more than one ingress controller — say an internal one and an internet-facing one — every Ingress needs to declare which should pick it up. IngressClass is that declaration target. Each controller installs an IngressClass whose `spec.controller` is a fixed identifier the controller recognises, such as `k8s.io/ingress-nginx`.

An Ingress then sets `spec.ingressClassName: nginx`, and only the controller owning that class acts on it. This replaced the old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation, which was never validated and silently did nothing when misspelled.

An IngressClass can be marked the cluster default with the annotation `ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`. Ingresses that specify no class then get assigned to it at admission time. Only one class should carry that annotation — with two, the API server rejects Ingresses that omit a class.

`spec.parameters` optionally points at a controller-specific configuration object, letting one controller offer several behaviour profiles as separate classes.
whenToUse: Any cluster running more than one ingress controller
Separating internal-only from internet-facing ingress
Setting a cluster-wide default so simple Ingresses need no class field
Usually installed for you by the controller's Helm chart rather than written by hand

keyFields.description: Identifier of the controller that implements this class, e.g. k8s.io/ingress-nginx. Immutable.
Optional reference to a controller-specific config resource.
Set to "true" to make this the default for Ingresses that omit ingressClassName.

example:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
spec:
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
commonMistakes: Marking two IngressClasses as default. Ingresses without an explicit class are then rejected.
Inventing a spec.controller string. It must exactly match what the installed controller watches for, or nothing happens.
Still using the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation on Ingress objects; newer controllers may ignore it entirely.
Trying to edit spec.controller on an existing class — it is immutable, so delete and recreate.
kubectlTips: kubectl get ingressclass -o wide  — see class names and their controllers
kubectl get ingressclass -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.metadata.annotations.ingressclass\.kubernetes\.io/is-default-class}{"\n"}{end}'  — find the default

summary: A firewall for Pods: says which traffic is allowed in and out, based on labels rather than IP addresses.
explanation:
By default every Pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other Pod, in every namespace. NetworkPolicy is how you stop that. It selects Pods by label and states which connections are permitted.

The model is additive allow-listing with an important twist. A Pod selected by no policy at all accepts everything. The moment any policy selects a Pod for a direction, that Pod becomes default-deny for that direction, and only traffic matching some policy is allowed. So creating one narrow ingress policy does not just add a rule — it flips that Pod from open to closed and then opens a hole. `spec.policyTypes` states which directions the policy governs; a policy with `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and an empty `egress` list denies all egress.

Rules match by `podSelector`, `namespaceSelector`, or `ipBlock` for CIDR ranges. Selectors work on labels, so policies survive Pod restarts and IP changes. Note the YAML subtlety: within one `from` entry, a `podSelector` and a `namespaceSelector` listed as fields of the same item mean AND, while two separate list items mean OR. That single dash changes the meaning completely.

NetworkPolicy is enforced by the CNI plugin, not by Kubernetes itself. Calico, Cilium and others implement it; Flannel on its own does not. On a cluster whose CNI ignores policies, they are accepted by the API server and enforce nothing — a silent and dangerous no-op.
whenToUse: Isolating namespaces so teams or tenants cannot reach each other
Restricting database Pods to only accept connections from the application tier
Meeting compliance requirements for network segmentation
Limiting egress so a compromised Pod cannot call out to arbitrary hosts

keyFields.description: Which Pods in this namespace the policy applies to. An empty selector {} selects every Pod in the namespace.
Ingress, Egress or both. Determines which directions become default-deny for the selected Pods.
Allowed sources: podSelector, namespaceSelector, or ipBlock.
Allowed destinations, same selector shapes.
Allowed ports and protocols. Omit to allow all ports from the listed sources.
CIDRs carved out of an otherwise allowed range — commonly used to block cloud metadata endpoints.

example:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-allow-api
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
commonMistakes: Running on a CNI that does not implement NetworkPolicy. The object applies cleanly and blocks nothing.
Adding an egress policy and forgetting to allow DNS to kube-dns on port 53. Every hostname lookup in the Pod fails and the app looks broken in confusing ways.
Writing '- podSelector' and '- namespaceSelector' as two list items when you meant AND. Two items mean OR, which allows far more than intended.
Expecting policies to filter by Service name or ClusterIP. Rules see Pod IPs, so you select the backend Pods, not the Service.
Assuming a policy in one namespace protects Pods in another. NetworkPolicy is namespaced and podSelector only sees its own namespace.
kubectlTips: kubectl get netpol -A  — a namespace with none is fully open
kubectl describe netpol db-allow-api -n production  — kubectl renders the allow rules in readable form
kubectl run probe --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://postgres:5432  — verify a policy actually blocks what you think

summary: The actual list of Pod IPs and ports behind a Service, split into manageable chunks.
explanation:
EndpointSlice is where a Service's backend addresses really live. The endpoints controller watches Pods matching a Service's selector and writes their IPs, ports and readiness state into EndpointSlice objects labelled `kubernetes.io/service-name: <service>`. `kube-proxy` reads those slices to program its routing rules.

It exists because the older Endpoints object stored every address for a Service in a single resource. For a Service with thousands of Pods that object became enormous, and any one Pod changing meant the whole thing was rewritten and pushed to every node. EndpointSlice caps each slice at 100 endpoints by default, so a change rewrites one small object instead of one huge one.

Each endpoint carries `conditions` — `ready`, `serving` and `terminating` — which is richer than the old model's binary ready/not-ready split. A Pod that is shutting down can be marked terminating but still serving, letting proxies drain connections gracefully rather than cutting them off.

Slices are normally created for you. You only write one by hand when you want a Service that points at addresses Kubernetes does not manage — an external database, say — in which case you create a Service with no selector and supply the slice yourself.
whenToUse: Debugging a Service that returns connection refused — check whether any endpoints exist
Pointing a Service at an external IP by creating a selectorless Service plus a hand-written slice
Understanding how kube-proxy learns about backends
Normally created automatically; rarely authored by hand

keyFields.description: IPv4, IPv6 or FQDN. A top-level field, not under spec. All addresses in a slice must be of this type.
The backend addresses, usually one Pod IP per endpoint.
Whether this endpoint should receive traffic.
Reference back to the Pod this endpoint represents.
Ports exposed, each with name, port and protocol.
Links the slice to its Service. Required for a hand-written slice to be picked up.

example:
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: external-db-1
  namespace: default
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: external-db
addressType: IPv4
ports:
  - name: postgres
    protocol: TCP
    port: 5432
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "192.0.2.42"
    conditions:
      ready: true
commonMistakes: Editing an auto-generated slice. The controller overwrites your changes within seconds.
Hand-writing a slice without the kubernetes.io/service-name label, so no Service ever picks it up.
Putting addressType under a spec block. EndpointSlice has no spec — addressType, ports and endpoints are all top-level.
Expecting a Service with a selector to use your manual slice. Remove the selector, or the controller will fight you.
kubectlTips: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web  — the slices behind one Service
kubectl get endpointslice web-abc12 -o yaml  — see per-endpoint ready/serving/terminating conditions
kubectl get endpointslices -A  — a quick census of Services with no backends

summary: The original, now-deprecated list of addresses behind a Service; EndpointSlice replaced it.
explanation:
**Legacy.** Endpoints is the first-generation backing list for a Service: one object, named identically to the Service, holding every backend address in a single `subsets` array. It was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.33 in favour of EndpointSlice.

The scaling problem is structural. Every address for a Service lives in one object, so a Service with 5,000 Pods produces a single very large resource, and one Pod becoming ready rewrites and redistributes the whole thing to every node. EndpointSlice splits the same data into chunks of 100.

For compatibility the control plane still mirrors EndpointSlices back into Endpoints objects, so old tooling keeps working — but only up to 1,000 addresses per Service, and the mirrored object is truncated beyond that with a `endpoints.kubernetes.io/over-capacity` annotation. Anything reading Endpoints on a large Service is therefore seeing an incomplete picture.

The one place it still shows up deliberately is the classic recipe for a selectorless Service pointing at an external host. That recipe now works equally well with EndpointSlice, which is what new material should use.
whenToUse: Reading older manifests, tutorials or controllers that still reference it
Nothing new — write EndpointSlice instead

keyFields.description: Ready backend addresses, each with an ip field.
Backends that exist but are not ready to serve.
Ports for the addresses in this subset.
Must exactly equal the Service name — that name match is the only link between the two.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Endpoints
metadata:
  name: external-db
  namespace: default
subsets:
  - addresses:
      - ip: "192.0.2.42"
    ports:
      - name: postgres
        port: 5432
        protocol: TCP
commonMistakes: Naming the Endpoints object something other than the Service. There is no selector or label linking them — only the name.
Reading Endpoints to enumerate backends on a large Service, and silently getting a list truncated at 1,000 addresses.
Building new controllers against Endpoints. Watch EndpointSlice instead; Endpoints is deprecated.
Creating an Endpoints object for a Service that still has a selector. The controller overwrites it immediately.
kubectlTips: kubectl get ep  — still the fastest one-line check for whether a Service has any backends
kubectl get ep web -o yaml  — compare against the EndpointSlices to see the mirroring in action

summary: Names an implementation of the Gateway API, the way IngressClass names an ingress controller.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** The Gateway API ships as a set of CustomResourceDefinitions maintained by the Kubernetes project but installed separately — you apply the CRD bundle before any of these kinds exist. `kubectl get gatewayclass` on a stock cluster returns "the server doesn't have a resource type".

GatewayClass is the cluster-scoped anchor of the model. It has essentially one meaningful field, `spec.controllerName`, a fixed identifier belonging to the implementation that should handle Gateways of this class — for example `istio.io/gateway-controller` or `projectcontour.io/gateway-controller`. The implementation's install manifests normally create the GatewayClass for you.

The division of labour is the point of the design. A cluster operator creates GatewayClasses; an infrastructure team creates Gateways referencing them; application teams create HTTPRoutes in their own namespaces that attach to a Gateway. Ingress squeezed all three roles into one object and one pile of annotations, which is precisely what this splits apart.

Check the `Accepted` condition in `status`. An unrecognised `controllerName` leaves the GatewayClass present but never accepted, and every Gateway pointing at it stays unprogrammed.
whenToUse: Installing a Gateway API implementation such as Istio, Contour, Envoy Gateway or Cilium
Offering several classes of gateway — internal and external, or different proxy tiers
Created by the implementation's install manifests far more often than by hand

keyFields.description: Identifier of the implementation that reconciles Gateways of this class. Immutable and must match exactly.
Optional reference to an implementation-specific configuration resource.
Human-readable description shown in kubectl output.
Look for Accepted=True; anything else means no Gateway of this class will be programmed.

example:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: external
spec:
  controllerName: example.net/gateway-controller
  description: Internet-facing gateways
commonMistakes: Applying Gateway API manifests before installing the CRDs, and getting 'no matches for kind' errors.
Guessing at controllerName. It must match the string the installed implementation watches, character for character.
Assuming an ingress controller supports Gateway API because it supports Ingress. Many need a separate component enabled.
Creating a GatewayClass in a namespace — it is cluster-scoped.
kubectlTips: kubectl get gatewayclass  — the ACCEPTED column tells you whether an implementation claimed it
kubectl get crd | grep gateway.networking  — confirm the Gateway API CRDs are installed at all

summary: Declares the actual entry point into the cluster: which ports, protocols and hostnames accept traffic.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** Gateway is a CustomResourceDefinition from the Gateway API project, installed separately from the cluster itself.

A Gateway is the successor to Ingress, split into pieces. It describes the listener side only: bind port 443, speak HTTPS, present this certificate, accept these hostnames. It says nothing about which path goes to which Service — that is the job of route objects such as HTTPRoute, which attach to the Gateway by reference. Creating a Gateway typically causes the implementation to provision a real load balancer and report its address in `status.addresses`.

Each entry in `spec.listeners` has a name, port, protocol, optional hostname, and a TLS block. `allowedRoutes` controls which routes may attach: `Same` restricts to the Gateway's own namespace, `All` permits any, and a `Selector` limits attachment to namespaces carrying particular labels. This is the mechanism that lets a platform team own the Gateway while application teams safely attach their own routes from their own namespaces — something Ingress could never express.

Cross-namespace references are deliberately not implicit. A route in another namespace attaching to this Gateway is governed by `allowedRoutes`; a Gateway referencing a TLS Secret in another namespace additionally needs a ReferenceGrant in the Secret's namespace. The default is always deny.
whenToUse: Replacing Ingress when you need annotation-free, portable configuration
Sharing one load balancer across teams with per-namespace route delegation
Routing protocols Ingress cannot express, such as raw TCP, UDP or gRPC
Traffic splitting for canaries expressed in the spec rather than in vendor annotations

keyFields.description: Which GatewayClass, and therefore which implementation, provisions this Gateway.
Unique listener name; routes reference it via sectionName when attaching.
Port the listener binds.
HTTP, HTTPS, TLS, TCP or UDP.
Hostname this listener accepts; wildcards like *.example.com are allowed.
Secrets holding TLS certificates. Cross-namespace refs require a ReferenceGrant.
Same, All or Selector — which namespaces may attach routes here.
The external address the implementation assigned.

example:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: external
  namespace: gateway-system
spec:
  gatewayClassName: external
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: All
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: "*.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - kind: Secret
            name: example-com-tls
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Selector
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              gateway-access: "true"
commonMistakes: Expecting a Gateway alone to route traffic. Without an HTTPRoute attached it listens and serves nothing.
Forgetting a ReferenceGrant for a TLS Secret or backend Service in another namespace, so the reference is silently refused.
Setting allowedRoutes to Same and then wondering why an application team's route in their own namespace never attaches.
Assuming Gateway API is installed. It is a separate CRD bundle that has to be applied first.
kubectlTips: kubectl get gateway -A  — the ADDRESS and PROGRAMMED columns show whether a real load balancer exists yet
kubectl describe gateway external -n gateway-system  — per-listener status shows attachedRoutes counts and rejection reasons

summary: HTTP routing rules that attach to a Gateway and send matching requests to Services.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** HTTPRoute is a CustomResourceDefinition from the Gateway API, installed alongside Gateway and GatewayClass.

An HTTPRoute is the rules half of what Ingress used to do in one object. It names the Gateway it attaches to in `spec.parentRefs`, optionally narrows to specific hostnames, and lists `rules` that match on path, headers, query parameters or method, then forward to `backendRefs`. The route lives in the application's namespace while the Gateway lives in the platform team's, which is the whole point of the split.

Two features that required vendor annotations under Ingress are first-class here. `backendRefs` accepts a `weight` on each entry, so a canary is `weight: 90` and `weight: 10` on two Services — portable across implementations. And `filters` express request and response manipulation directly: `RequestHeaderModifier`, `RequestRedirect`, `URLRewrite` and `RequestMirror` are all part of the standard spec.

Matching is specified rather than left to the implementation. Rules are evaluated by precedence — exact path beats path prefix, longer prefix beats shorter, more header matches beat fewer — so two implementations should route identically, unlike the annotation-driven Ingress world. Attaching across namespaces is allowed only if the Gateway's `allowedRoutes` permits it, and forwarding to a Service in another namespace additionally requires a ReferenceGrant in that namespace.
whenToUse: Path- and header-based routing on a Gateway API cluster
Weighted traffic splitting for canary and blue/green releases
Header rewriting, redirects and request mirroring without vendor annotations
Letting application teams manage their own routes on a shared gateway

keyFields.description: The Gateway (and optionally the listener via sectionName) this route attaches to.
Hostnames this route serves; intersected with the listener's hostname.
Conditions on path, headers, query params or method. Multiple matches in one rule are OR-ed.
Target Service name; port is required.
Relative share of traffic across backends in the rule — the built-in canary control.
RequestHeaderModifier, RequestRedirect, URLRewrite, RequestMirror and friends.
Accepted and ResolvedRefs per parent Gateway — where attachment failures are reported.

example:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: default
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: external
      namespace: gateway-system
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - shop.example.com
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /api
      filters:
        - type: RequestHeaderModifier
          requestHeaderModifier:
            set:
              - name: X-Forwarded-Prefix
                value: /api
      backendRefs:
        - name: api
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: api-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        - name: web
          port: 80
commonMistakes: Omitting the namespace in parentRefs when the Gateway lives elsewhere. It defaults to the route's own namespace and attachment silently fails.
Forwarding to a Service in another namespace without a ReferenceGrant there — ResolvedRefs goes False and traffic 500s.
Setting hostnames that do not intersect the listener's hostname, so the route attaches but matches nothing.
Expecting weights to be percentages. They are relative shares; 1 and 3 means 25% and 75%.
Forgetting port on a backendRef — it is required, unlike some Ingress controllers' defaults.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe httproute shop  — the Parents section shows Accepted and ResolvedRefs, which is where attachment problems appear
kubectl get httproute -A  — inventory every route and the Gateways they claim
kubectl get gateway external -n gateway-system -o jsonpath='{.status.listeners[*].attachedRoutes}'  — confirm the Gateway sees your route

summary: Holds non-secret configuration as key/value pairs that Pods read as environment variables or files.
explanation:
A ConfigMap keeps configuration out of the container image, so the same image can run in dev, staging and production with different settings. It is a flat map of string keys to string values under `data`, plus `binaryData` for base64-encoded binary content. Total size is capped at roughly 1 MiB, because the object lives in etcd.

There are two ways to consume one, and they behave very differently. As environment variables (`env.valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` or `envFrom.configMapRef`) the values are copied into the process at container start and then frozen — editing the ConfigMap changes nothing until the Pod is recreated. As a mounted volume, the kubelet writes each key as a file in the mount directory and refreshes those files in place when the ConfigMap changes, typically within a minute or two. The file contents update, but your application still has to notice and reload; most do not.

A subtlety with volume mounts: mounting a ConfigMap over a directory replaces the whole directory. Use `subPath` to place a single file into an existing directory instead — but a `subPath` mount is a one-time copy and never receives updates, trading live reload for coexistence with other files.

Setting `immutable: true` locks the contents. That is not just safety: the kubelet stops watching immutable ConfigMaps, which meaningfully reduces API server load in large clusters. To change an immutable ConfigMap you create a new one under a different name and point the Pod template at it — which conveniently also triggers a rollout.
whenToUse: Application settings that differ per environment: log levels, feature flags, endpoints
Full configuration files such as nginx.conf, application.yaml or prometheus.yml
Command-line arguments and non-sensitive environment variables
Never for passwords, tokens or keys — use a Secret

keyFields.description: String key/value pairs. Keys become environment variable names or filenames.
Base64-encoded values for binary content that is not valid UTF-8.
Set true to forbid updates and let the kubelet stop watching the object.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
  namespace: default
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  MAX_CONNECTIONS: "100"
  app.yaml: |
    server:
      port: 8080
      timeout: 30s
    features:
      newCheckout: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "cat /etc/app/app.yaml && sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
      volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/app
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: config
      configMap:
        name: app-config
commonMistakes: Expecting environment variables to update when the ConfigMap changes. They never do — the Pod must be recreated.
Storing credentials in a ConfigMap. There is no access-control distinction from ordinary config, and it will end up in logs and Git.
Using subPath and then wondering why live updates stopped. subPath mounts are copies and are never refreshed.
Unquoted numeric or boolean values in data. YAML parses 'true' as a boolean and the API rejects it — every value must be a string.
Mounting a ConfigMap at /etc and shadowing the entire directory, breaking DNS resolution inside the container.
kubectlTips: kubectl create configmap app-config --from-file=app.yaml --dry-run=client -o yaml  — generate correct YAML from a real file
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug  — quick key/value creation
kubectl rollout restart deploy/web  — the standard way to pick up a changed ConfigMap consumed as env vars
kubectl get cm app-config -o jsonpath='{.data.app\.yaml}'  — print one key's contents

summary: Holds sensitive values such as passwords, tokens and TLS keys, kept separate from ordinary config.
explanation:
A Secret is structurally almost identical to a ConfigMap — a small map of keys to values, consumed as environment variables or mounted files — but it is treated differently by the platform. Values are base64-encoded in the object (encoding, not encryption), the kubelet keeps mounted Secrets in memory-backed tmpfs rather than on node disk, and RBAC rules commonly grant Secret access far more narrowly than ConfigMap access.

Base64 is not a security measure; anyone who can read the object can read the value. Real protection comes from three places: RBAC that limits who can `get` Secrets in a namespace, encryption at rest configured on the API server (`EncryptionConfiguration`, off by default in many distributions), and keeping Secrets out of Git — via Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or a cloud secret manager mounted through the CSI Secrets Store driver.

The `type` field is meaningful, not decorative. `Opaque` is the free-form default. `kubernetes.io/tls` requires exactly the keys `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, and is what Ingress and Gateway TLS references expect. `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` requires `.dockerconfigjson` and is what `imagePullSecrets` consumes. The API server validates required keys per type, so a mistyped key is caught at apply time.

Write plaintext under `stringData` and let the API server do the base64 encoding — it is write-only and appears as `data` when you read the object back. Note that a Pod granted a Secret as an env var exposes it to anything that can read `/proc/<pid>/environ` or run `kubectl describe pod`; a file mount is generally the safer consumption path.
whenToUse: Database passwords, API tokens and OAuth client secrets
TLS certificates and private keys for Ingress or Gateway listeners
Registry credentials for pulling private images
ServiceAccount tokens when a long-lived token is genuinely required

keyFields.description: Opaque, kubernetes.io/tls, kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, kubernetes.io/basic-auth and others. Determines which keys are required.
Base64-encoded values.
Plaintext values, encoded by the API server on write. Write-only — reads always show data.
Set true to forbid updates and reduce kubelet watch load.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-credentials
  namespace: default
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: appuser
  password: "s3cr3t-example-value"
  url: "postgres://appuser:s3cr3t-example-value@postgres:5432/app"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
      env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: db-credentials
              key: password
      volumeMounts:
        - name: creds
          mountPath: /etc/creds
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: creds
      secret:
        secretName: db-credentials
        defaultMode: 0400
commonMistakes: Believing base64 encodes secrecy. `kubectl get secret -o yaml | base64 -d` is all it takes to read one.
Committing Secret manifests to Git. Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets or a CSI secret store instead.
Putting a trailing newline in the value — `echo password | base64` includes it, and authentication then fails mysteriously. Use `echo -n` or stringData.
Assuming Secrets are encrypted at rest. They are stored in plain etcd unless EncryptionConfiguration is explicitly enabled.
Granting a ServiceAccount `list` on Secrets in a namespace, which in practice means reading every credential in it.
kubectlTips: kubectl create secret generic db-credentials --from-literal=password=hunter2 --dry-run=client -o yaml  — generate a manifest without shell-escaping pain
kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key  — build a correctly typed TLS Secret
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...  — registry pull credentials
kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d  — read one value back

summary: A piece of real storage in the cluster — a cloud disk, an NFS export — represented as an API object.
explanation:
A PersistentVolume is the supply side of storage. It represents an actual volume that exists somewhere: an EBS volume, a GCE disk, an NFS export, a Ceph image. It is cluster-scoped, because storage exists independently of any namespace, and it has a lifecycle separate from any Pod that uses it.

PVs are matched to PersistentVolumeClaims by the control plane. A claim states what it needs — size, access mode, storage class — and the binder finds or provisions a PV that satisfies it. Binding is exclusive and one-to-one: once a PV is bound to a claim, no other claim can use it, even if the PV is much larger than requested. The PV then moves through phases: Available, Bound, Released (claim deleted but not yet reclaimed), and Failed.

Most PVs today are created automatically by dynamic provisioning: a PVC names a StorageClass, the CSI driver creates a real disk, and a matching PV appears without anyone writing one. You write PVs by hand mainly for pre-existing storage such as an NFS share, or in learning clusters using `hostPath`.

`persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy` decides what happens when the claim is deleted. `Delete` destroys the underlying storage — the default for dynamically provisioned volumes, and a genuine data-loss hazard. `Retain` keeps both the PV and the data, leaving the PV in Released state where it will not rebind until an administrator clears `spec.claimRef` manually. Access modes describe how many nodes may mount it: `ReadWriteOnce` (one node, the common case for block storage), `ReadOnlyMany`, `ReadWriteMany` (needs a shared filesystem such as NFS or CephFS), and `ReadWriteOncePod`, which restricts access to exactly one Pod.
whenToUse: Exposing existing NFS, iSCSI or SMB storage to the cluster
Pre-provisioning specific volumes an administrator controls
Local-disk PVs pinned to particular nodes for latency-sensitive workloads
Rarely by hand otherwise — dynamic provisioning via StorageClass creates them for you

keyFields.description: Size of the volume. Used for matching claims; it does not resize anything.
ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany or ReadWriteOncePod.
Retain, Delete or the deprecated Recycle. Decides the fate of the data when the claim goes away.
Class name used to match claims. Empty string means no class.
The volume source — exactly one backend type per PV.
The PVC this PV is bound to. Clear it to make a Released PV bindable again.
Restricts which nodes can mount the volume. Required for local volumes.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: nfs-shared
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 100Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: nfs
  mountOptions:
    - hard
    - nfsvers=4.1
  nfs:
    server: 192.0.2.10
    path: /exports/shared
commonMistakes: Leaving the reclaim policy at Delete on data you care about. Deleting the PVC silently destroys the cloud disk.
Expecting a Released PV to rebind automatically. It will not until spec.claimRef is cleared.
Requesting ReadWriteMany on block storage such as EBS. It only supports ReadWriteOnce and the Pod stays Pending.
Using hostPath PVs in a multi-node cluster. The data lives on one node and the Pod may be scheduled elsewhere.
Assuming a 100Gi PV can serve a 10Gi claim and leave room for another. Binding is exclusive — the rest is wasted.
kubectlTips: kubectl get pv  — STATUS and CLAIM columns show what is bound to what
kubectl get pv --sort-by=.spec.capacity.storage  — find the large volumes
kubectl patch pv nfs-shared -p '{"spec":{"claimRef":null}}'  — make a Released PV available again
kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,POLICY:.spec.persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy  — audit reclaim policies before something gets deleted

summary: A request for storage: how much, what access mode, what class — the cluster finds or creates it.
explanation:
A PersistentVolumeClaim is the demand side of storage. Instead of naming a specific disk, a Pod names a claim, and the claim describes requirements: 10Gi, ReadWriteOnce, class `fast-ssd`. The control plane binds the claim to a suitable PersistentVolume, or asks the StorageClass's provisioner to create one. This indirection is what lets the same manifest run on EKS, GKE and a laptop cluster — only the StorageClass differs.

Binding timing is set by the StorageClass's `volumeBindingMode`. With `Immediate`, a volume is provisioned as soon as the claim is created, before anyone knows where the Pod will run — which on a zonal cloud disk can strand the Pod in the wrong availability zone forever. With `WaitForFirstConsumer`, provisioning waits until a Pod using the claim is scheduled, so the volume lands in the right zone and on the right node. The second is nearly always what you want.

Omitting `storageClassName` is not the same as setting it to `""`. Omitting it means "use the cluster default class"; the empty string means "do not use dynamic provisioning at all, bind only to a pre-created PV with no class". Confusing the two produces a claim stuck in Pending with no obvious explanation.

Claims can be grown if the StorageClass sets `allowVolumeExpansion: true` — edit `spec.resources.requests.storage` upward and the driver expands the volume, with filesystem expansion happening on next mount or online depending on the driver. Shrinking is never supported.
whenToUse: Any Pod that needs data to survive a restart or reschedule
Databases, message queues and anything with on-disk state
Inside a StatefulSet's volumeClaimTemplates for per-replica storage
Shared read-write storage across Pods, if the backend supports ReadWriteMany

keyFields.description: Required. ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany or ReadWriteOncePod.
How much space to request. Increase it to expand, if the class allows expansion.
Class to provision from. Omit for the cluster default; set "" to disable dynamic provisioning.
Bind to one specific PV by name, bypassing normal matching.
Create the volume from a VolumeSnapshot or clone an existing PVC.
Pending or Bound. A long-Pending claim is the classic symptom of a missing or mismatched StorageClass.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-data
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
  namespace: default
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: app-data
commonMistakes: A Pending PVC because no default StorageClass exists in the cluster. kubectl describe pvc shows it immediately.
Setting storageClassName: "" thinking it means 'default'. It means 'no dynamic provisioning', and the claim never binds.
Trying to shrink a claim. Only expansion is supported, and only when the class allows it.
Mounting one ReadWriteOnce claim into a multi-replica Deployment. Pods on other nodes stay stuck at ContainerCreating.
Deleting a PVC bound to a Delete-policy PV and losing the underlying disk along with the data.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe pvc app-data  — the Events section names the exact provisioning failure
kubectl get pvc -A  — hunt for Pending claims across the cluster
kubectl patch pvc app-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'  — expand a volume in place
kubectl get pvc app-data -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}'  — find the PV behind a claim

summary: A named recipe for creating storage on demand — which driver, what disk type, what settings.
explanation:
A StorageClass turns "I need 10Gi" into an actual disk. It names a provisioner (a CSI driver) and the parameters to hand it, so a claim referencing the class gets a volume built to that recipe. Clusters typically offer several: `standard` for cheap disks, `fast-ssd` for low-latency ones, `nfs` for shared filesystems. Note the object's unusual shape: it has no `spec`. `provisioner`, `parameters`, `reclaimPolicy`, `volumeBindingMode` and `allowVolumeExpansion` are all top-level fields. This trips up nearly everyone writing one for the first time.

`volumeBindingMode` is the field that matters most in practice. `Immediate` provisions the volume the moment a claim appears, which on multi-zone clouds regularly creates the disk in a zone with no capacity for the Pod, leaving it unschedulable forever. `WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until the scheduler has picked a node, so topology matches by construction. Prefer it unless you have a specific reason not to.

`reclaimPolicy` here becomes the reclaim policy of every PV the class provisions, and it defaults to `Delete`. For anything holding real data, a `Retain` class is worth having. `allowVolumeExpansion: true` is required for PVCs of this class to be growable — and it cannot be applied retroactively to volumes already created, since most fields on an existing StorageClass are immutable; changing the recipe means creating a new class.

The annotation `storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"` makes a class the cluster default, used by any PVC that omits `storageClassName`.
whenToUse: Offering tiers of storage: cheap bulk versus fast SSD
