Setting a cluster default so simple PVCs just work
Providing a Retain-policy class for data that must survive claim deletion
Configuring encryption, IOPS, throughput or filesystem type per driver

keyFields.description: CSI driver name, e.g. ebs.csi.aws.com or pd.csi.storage.gke.io. Top-level, not under spec.
Driver-specific settings such as type, iops, encrypted or fsType.
Delete (default) or Retain — inherited by every PV this class creates.
Immediate or WaitForFirstConsumer. The latter avoids zone-mismatch scheduling failures.
Whether PVCs of this class can be grown. Must be set before the volume is created.
Restrict provisioning to particular zones or node groups.
Set to "true" for the cluster default class.

example:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
  encrypted: "true"
  fsType: ext4
reclaimPolicy: Retain
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
commonMistakes: Wrapping the fields in a spec block. StorageClass has no spec and the manifest will be rejected.
Leaving volumeBindingMode at Immediate on a multi-zone cluster, producing volumes in zones where the Pod cannot run.
Forgetting allowVolumeExpansion until a disk fills up. It cannot be applied to volumes already provisioned.
Marking two classes as default, which makes PVCs without an explicit class ambiguous.
Trying to edit provisioner or parameters on an existing class. Most fields are immutable; create a new class instead.
kubectlTips: kubectl get sc  — the (default) marker appears next to the default class name
kubectl get sc -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,POLICY:.reclaimPolicy,EXPAND:.allowVolumeExpansion  — audit the classes at a glance
kubectl patch sc standard -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"false"}}}'  — demote a default class

summary: A point-in-time copy of a PersistentVolumeClaim's data, which you can restore into a new claim.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** VolumeSnapshot is a CustomResourceDefinition from the external CSI snapshotter project. You must install the snapshot CRDs and the snapshot-controller separately, and the CSI driver must support snapshots. On a cluster without them, `kubectl get volumesnapshot` reports an unknown resource type.

Creating a VolumeSnapshot asks the CSI driver to take a point-in-time snapshot of the volume backing a PVC. The namespaced VolumeSnapshot you create is paired with a cluster-scoped VolumeSnapshotContent representing the real snapshot in the storage system — the same two-object split as PVC and PV, for the same reason.

Restoring goes through `dataSource` on a new PVC: reference the snapshot by name and kind `VolumeSnapshot`, and the provisioner creates a fresh volume pre-populated with that data. The restored claim must be at least as large as the original, and must use a class backed by the same driver.

Snapshots are usually incremental and stored by the storage backend, not by Kubernetes. They are therefore not backups in the disaster-recovery sense: they typically live in the same storage system as the original, so losing the backend loses both. Treat them as fast rollback points, and keep real backups elsewhere. One operational caveat: a snapshot captures the block device, not application state. A database snapshotted mid-write restores to a crash-consistent state, so quiesce the application or use its own backup tooling when consistency matters.
whenToUse: Taking a rollback point immediately before a risky migration
Cloning production data into a staging environment
Fast recovery from an accidental delete or bad write
Not as your only backup — snapshots usually share the fate of the underlying storage

keyFields.description: The PVC to snapshot. Must be in the same namespace.
Alternative source: bind to a pre-existing snapshot content object.
Which VolumeSnapshotClass, and therefore which driver and deletion policy, to use.
Whether the snapshot is complete. Restoring before this is true will fail.
The cluster-scoped content object holding the real snapshot.

example:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: app-data-before-migration
  namespace: default
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: csi-snapclass
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: app-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: app-data-restored
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: standard
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
  dataSource:
    name: app-data-before-migration
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
commonMistakes: Assuming snapshots work out of the box. The CRDs, the snapshot-controller and CSI driver support all have to be installed.
Treating snapshots as backups. They usually live in the same storage backend as the source volume.
Restoring into a smaller PVC than the original. The claim stays Pending.
Snapshotting a running database without quiescing it, then discovering the restore is only crash-consistent.
Forgetting apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io in the PVC dataSource, so the reference does not resolve.
kubectlTips: kubectl get volumesnapshot  — READYTOUSE tells you whether it is safe to restore from
kubectl get volumesnapshotcontent  — the cluster-scoped side, useful when a snapshot is stuck
kubectl describe volumesnapshot app-data-before-migration  — driver errors surface in Events

summary: A named recipe for taking snapshots: which CSI driver, and whether deleting the snapshot deletes the data.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** Like VolumeSnapshot, this is a CRD from the external CSI snapshotter project and must be installed separately.

VolumeSnapshotClass is to snapshots what StorageClass is to volumes. It names the CSI `driver` that takes the snapshot, a `deletionPolicy`, and any driver-specific `parameters`. It shares StorageClass's unusual shape: no `spec` block, everything at the top level.

`deletionPolicy` is the field with teeth. `Delete` means removing the VolumeSnapshot object also removes the underlying snapshot in the storage backend. `Retain` keeps the backend snapshot and leaves the VolumeSnapshotContent behind for manual handling. For anything you might need to restore from later, `Retain` avoids an irreversible mistake.

A class can be marked default with the annotation `snapshot.storage.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"`, in which case VolumeSnapshots omitting `volumeSnapshotClassName` use it. The `driver` must match the CSI driver backing the volume being snapshotted — you cannot snapshot an EBS volume with a Ceph snapshot class.
whenToUse: Setting up snapshot support for a CSI driver in the cluster
Offering a Retain-policy class for snapshots that must outlive their objects
Passing driver-specific options such as incremental snapshot settings
Usually installed by the storage driver's Helm chart

keyFields.description: CSI driver name that takes the snapshot. Top-level field; must match the volume's provisioner.
Delete or Retain. Required — decides whether the backend snapshot is destroyed with the object.
Driver-specific snapshot options.
Set to "true" to make this the default snapshot class.

example:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: csi-snapclass
  annotations:
    snapshot.storage.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
deletionPolicy: Retain
commonMistakes: Putting driver and deletionPolicy under a spec block. There is no spec on this object.
Leaving deletionPolicy at Delete and losing the backend snapshot when tidying up objects.
Using a class whose driver differs from the volume's provisioner — the snapshot never becomes ready.
Omitting deletionPolicy entirely; it is a required field.
kubectlTips: kubectl get volumesnapshotclass  — shows driver and deletion policy per class
kubectl get volumesnapshotclass -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,DRIVER:.driver,POLICY:.deletionPolicy  — audit before relying on one

summary: Registers a storage driver with the cluster and tells Kubernetes how to interact with it.
explanation:
The Container Storage Interface is the plugin standard that let storage vendors stop shipping code inside Kubernetes itself. The in-tree cloud volume plugins were all removed in favour of CSI drivers running as ordinary Pods — usually a controller Deployment plus a node DaemonSet.

The CSIDriver object is the registration record. Its `metadata.name` must be exactly the driver name used as `provisioner` in StorageClasses, such as `ebs.csi.aws.com`. Its fields tell the kubelet and attach/detach controller how to behave: whether volumes need an attach step, whether the driver wants Pod identity information at mount time, which lifecycle modes it supports, and how fsGroup ownership changes should be applied.

`attachRequired` is significant. Set false for drivers with no attach phase — NFS-style network filesystems — and Kubernetes skips creating VolumeAttachment objects, which removes a whole class of stuck-detach failures. Block-storage drivers set it true. `volumeLifecycleModes` declares whether the driver supports normal `Persistent` volumes, `Ephemeral` inline volumes defined directly in a Pod spec, or both. The Secrets Store CSI driver, for example, is ephemeral-only.

You almost never write this object; the driver's install manifests do. It is worth knowing because it is where you look when a driver is misbehaving, and because `kubectl get csidrivers` is the quickest way to see what storage a cluster can actually provision.
whenToUse: Installing a storage driver — its manifests create this for you
Diagnosing why volumes fail to attach or mount
Checking which drivers a cluster supports before writing a StorageClass
Rarely authored by hand

keyFields.description: The driver name. Must match the provisioner field in StorageClasses exactly.
Whether volumes need a separate attach step and VolumeAttachment objects.
Pass Pod name, namespace and ServiceAccount to the driver at mount time — needed by drivers doing per-Pod authorization.
Persistent, Ephemeral, or both.
ReadWriteOnceWithFSType (default), File or None — controls whether the kubelet chowns the volume for fsGroup.
Whether the driver publishes CSIStorageCapacity objects so the scheduler can avoid full storage pools.

example:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: CSIDriver
metadata:
  name: nfs.csi.k8s.io
spec:
  attachRequired: false
  podInfoOnMount: true
  storageCapacity: false
  fsGroupPolicy: File
  volumeLifecycleModes:
    - Persistent
commonMistakes: A StorageClass provisioner that does not match any installed CSIDriver name. PVCs stay Pending with a provisioning error.
Setting attachRequired: true for a network filesystem driver, adding a pointless attach phase that can hang.
Editing the object by hand and having the driver's install manifests revert it on the next upgrade.
Expecting old in-tree volume types such as awsElasticBlockStore in a Pod spec to still work — those plugins were removed.
kubectlTips: kubectl get csidrivers  — the definitive list of storage backends this cluster can use
kubectl get csinodes -o wide  — which drivers each node has actually registered
kubectl get volumeattachments  — where stuck attach and detach operations show up

summary: A named partition of the cluster that scopes object names, quotas and access control.
explanation:
A Namespace is a virtual boundary inside one cluster. Object names must be unique within a namespace but not across the cluster, so `web` in `staging` and `web` in `production` are different Deployments. It gives you a unit to attach RBAC, ResourceQuota, LimitRange and NetworkPolicy to — which is what makes it useful rather than merely tidy.

Not everything is namespaced. Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, ClusterRoles, CRDs and IngressClasses are cluster-scoped and exist once for the whole cluster. `kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false` lists them. Namespaces do not isolate the network. Pods in different namespaces reach each other freely by default; the only difference is DNS, where a name resolves within your own namespace unless you use the full `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` form. Real isolation requires NetworkPolicy.

Every cluster starts with four: `default`, `kube-system` (control-plane components), `kube-public` (world-readable cluster info) and `kube-node-lease` (node heartbeat Leases). Deleting a namespace deletes everything in it, asynchronously, via a finalizer. A namespace stuck in `Terminating` almost always means some resource in it has a finalizer that no controller is left alive to clear — commonly a CRD whose operator was uninstalled first.

Since Kubernetes 1.21 every namespace is automatically labelled `kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <name>`, which is what NetworkPolicy `namespaceSelector` rules usually match on. Pod Security Admission is also configured through labels here.
whenToUse: Separating environments or teams inside a shared cluster
Scoping RBAC so a team can only act on its own resources
Applying resource quotas per team or per tenant
Grouping an application's objects so they can be deleted together

keyFields.description: The namespace name — a DNS label, so lowercase alphanumerics and dashes.
Used by NetworkPolicy namespaceSelectors and by Pod Security Admission configuration.
Must be empty before deletion completes. A stuck Terminating namespace usually has one left.
Active or Terminating.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: production
  labels:
    environment: production
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
commonMistakes: Assuming namespaces isolate network traffic. They do not — add NetworkPolicy.
Deleting a namespace to clean up and taking out PVCs, and with them the underlying disks, as collateral.
Uninstalling an operator before deleting its custom resources, leaving the namespace stuck in Terminating on an unresolvable finalizer.
Expecting a Secret or ConfigMap to be visible across namespaces. They are not; each namespace needs its own copy.
Forgetting -n on kubectl and quietly operating on default instead of the intended namespace.
kubectlTips: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=production  — stop typing -n on every command
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false  — the definitive list of cluster-scoped kinds
kubectl get ns production -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers}'  — first thing to check on a stuck Terminating namespace
kubectl get all -n production  — a partial summary; note it omits Secrets, ConfigMaps, PVCs and Ingresses

summary: An identity for Pods, so workloads can authenticate to the Kubernetes API as themselves.
explanation:
Kubernetes has two kinds of identity. Human users come from outside — certificates, OIDC, cloud IAM — and there is no User object in the API. Workloads use ServiceAccounts, which are real, namespaced API objects, and are the only identity Kubernetes itself issues.

Every namespace automatically gets a ServiceAccount called `default`, and every Pod that does not name one gets it. That default account has essentially no permissions, which is deliberate: a Pod that never talks to the API needs none. Give a Pod a dedicated ServiceAccount whenever it does need access, and bind exactly the permissions it needs with a Role and RoleBinding.

Since Kubernetes 1.24 the token mechanics changed in an important way. ServiceAccounts no longer get a permanent Secret containing a never-expiring token. Instead the kubelet requests a short-lived, audience-bound token through the TokenRequest API and projects it into the Pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token`, rotating it automatically before expiry. Long-lived token Secrets can still be created explicitly with `type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token`, but they are a legacy escape hatch for tooling that cannot refresh.

Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or the Pod when a workload has no business calling the API — most application containers do not. That removes a credential from the container filesystem and closes an easy privilege-escalation path if the app is compromised. ServiceAccounts are also the anchor for cloud workload identity: annotate one with an AWS IAM role or GCP service account, and the projected token is exchanged for cloud credentials without any static keys.
whenToUse: Any Pod that calls the Kubernetes API — controllers, operators, CI runners
Binding cloud IAM identity to a workload via annotations (IRSA, Workload Identity)
Giving each application its own identity so RBAC can be scoped tightly
Attaching imagePullSecrets so every Pod using the account can pull private images

keyFields.description: Set false to stop mounting an API token into Pods using this account. Top-level field, not under spec.
Registry credentials automatically added to Pods using this ServiceAccount.
Legacy list of associated Secrets. No longer auto-populated since 1.24.
Where cloud workload-identity bindings live, e.g. eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: backup-agent
  namespace: default
automountServiceAccountToken: true
imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: backup-agent
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceAccountName: backup-agent
  containers:
    - name: agent
      image: bitnami/kubectl:1.31
      command: ["sh", "-c", "kubectl get pods && sleep 3600"]
commonMistakes: Leaving Pods on the default ServiceAccount and then granting the default account broad permissions — every Pod in the namespace inherits them.
Looking for an auto-created token Secret. Since 1.24 there is none; the token is projected by the kubelet instead.
Automounting API tokens into application Pods that never call the API, handing an attacker a free credential.
Assuming creating a ServiceAccount grants anything. On its own it has no permissions until a binding references it.
Referencing a ServiceAccount from another namespace in spec.serviceAccountName. It must exist in the Pod's own namespace.
kubectlTips: kubectl create sa backup-agent  — create one quickly
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:default:backup-agent  — test its permissions exactly as the API server would
kubectl create token backup-agent --duration=1h  — mint a short-lived token for debugging
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,SA:.spec.serviceAccountName  — audit which Pods use which identity

summary: A list of permissions inside one namespace — which verbs are allowed on which resources.
explanation:
A Role is a permission set, and nothing more. It grants nothing by itself: it has to be attached to a subject by a RoleBinding. Splitting the two means one Role can be reused for many users and ServiceAccounts.

Each rule combines three lists: `apiGroups`, `resources` and `verbs`. The core group is written as the empty string `""` — that is where Pods, Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets live. Everything else names its group: `apps` for Deployments, `batch` for Jobs, `networking.k8s.io` for Ingresses. Getting the group wrong is the most common reason a Role appears correct and grants nothing.

Resources are the plural, lowercase URL names — `pods`, not `Pod`. Subresources use a slash: `pods/log` for reading logs, `pods/exec` for shelling in, `deployments/scale` for scaling. Note that `get` on `pods` does not include `pods/log`; they are separate resources and must be listed separately.

RBAC is purely additive. There are no deny rules, so permissions can only accumulate; you restrict by granting less, never by subtracting. Verbs `create`, `update` and `patch` on a resource are all distinct — a subject with only `update` cannot `patch`, and server-side apply requires `patch`. `resourceNames` narrows a rule to specific named objects, which is how you grant read access to one Secret rather than all of them. It has a real limitation: it cannot restrict `list` or `watch`, because those operate on collections rather than named objects.
whenToUse: Giving an application read access to ConfigMaps in its own namespace
Letting a CI ServiceAccount deploy only within one namespace
Granting a team edit rights in their namespace and nothing else
Any permission that should stop at the namespace boundary

keyFields.description: API groups the rule covers. Use "" for the core group (pods, services, secrets).
Plural lowercase resource names, plus subresources like pods/log and pods/exec.
get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection — or * for all.
Restrict the rule to named objects. Cannot restrict list or watch.

example:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: config-reader
  namespace: default
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["secrets"]
    resourceNames: ["db-credentials"]
    verbs: ["get"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get"]
commonMistakes: Omitting apiGroups: [""] for core resources, or putting Deployments in the core group instead of apps. The rule then matches nothing.
Writing resources in singular or capitalised form. It must be pods, not Pod or pod.
Granting get on pods and expecting kubectl logs to work. That needs pods/log as a separate resource.
Using resourceNames and expecting it to filter a list. List and watch ignore resourceNames entirely.
Looking for a deny rule. RBAC has none — remove the grant instead.
kubectlTips: kubectl create role config-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=configmaps --dry-run=client -o yaml  — generate correct group names automatically
kubectl api-resources -o wide  — the APIVERSION and VERBS columns give you the exact strings a Role needs
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:default:app  — verify the result

summary: A permission set that is not tied to a namespace — for cluster-wide resources, or for reuse everywhere.
explanation:
A ClusterRole holds the same kind of rules as a Role but exists at cluster scope. It is needed for two distinct jobs, and confusing them causes most RBAC mistakes. First, cluster-scoped resources. Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, Namespaces and CRDs do not live in any namespace, so a namespaced Role can never grant access to them. Only a ClusterRole can. It is also the only way to grant access to non-resource URLs such as `/healthz` and `/metrics`, via `nonResourceURLs`.

Second, reuse. A ClusterRole defining "read Pods and Deployments" can be bound by a RoleBinding inside a single namespace, and the permissions then apply only there. So the same ClusterRole can be granted cluster-wide to one subject and namespace-locally to another. What decides the scope is the binding, not the role.

Every cluster ships with defaults worth knowing: `view` (read-only, excluding Secrets), `edit` (read/write on most namespaced resources), `admin` (edit plus RBAC management inside a namespace) and `cluster-admin` (everything, everywhere). Prefer binding these to writing your own for common cases.

`aggregationRule` lets a ClusterRole be assembled automatically from others: it selects ClusterRoles by label, and a controller merges their rules into this one's `rules` field. The built-in `view`, `edit` and `admin` roles use this, which is how a newly installed operator can extend `edit` with permissions on its own CRDs just by labelling a ClusterRole. Never write `rules` by hand on an aggregated role — the controller overwrites them.
whenToUse: Granting access to cluster-scoped resources like Nodes, PVs or CRDs
Permissions that must span every namespace, such as a monitoring agent's read access
Defining a reusable permission set to bind per-namespace with RoleBindings
Extending the built-in view/edit/admin roles via aggregation labels

keyFields.description: API groups covered. "" is the core group.
Plural resource names, including cluster-scoped ones like nodes and persistentvolumes.
The allowed operations.
Raw API paths such as /healthz or /metrics. Only valid in a ClusterRole.
Label selectors identifying ClusterRoles whose rules are merged into this one automatically.

example:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes", "nodes/status"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - apiGroups: ["storage.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["storageclasses", "csidrivers"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  - nonResourceURLs: ["/healthz", "/metrics"]
    verbs: ["get"]
commonMistakes: Binding cluster-admin because a narrower role was inconvenient — that grants full control of the cluster to the workload.
Expecting a RoleBinding to a ClusterRole to grant cluster-wide access. It grants only within the binding's namespace.
Writing rules by hand on a ClusterRole that has an aggregationRule. The aggregation controller overwrites them.
Trying to grant access to Nodes with a namespaced Role. Cluster-scoped resources need a ClusterRole.
Adding nonResourceURLs to a Role. The field only exists on ClusterRoles.
kubectlTips: kubectl get clusterrole  — long list; the system: prefixed ones are built in
kubectl describe clusterrole edit  — see exactly what the common built-in grants
kubectl get clusterrole view -o yaml  — a good template when writing your own read-only role
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:kube-system:agent  — everything a subject can do

summary: Grants the permissions in a Role or ClusterRole to specific users, groups or ServiceAccounts, within one namespace.
explanation:
A RoleBinding is the connection between a permission set and the people or workloads that get it. It has two halves: `roleRef`, naming exactly one Role or ClusterRole, and `subjects`, listing who receives the permissions.

The scope rule is the one thing to internalise. A RoleBinding always grants within its own namespace, regardless of what it references. Referencing a Role gives permissions on that namespace's resources. Referencing a ClusterRole gives that ClusterRole's permissions *but only inside this namespace* — which is how one `view` ClusterRole serves every namespace, bound separately in each. To grant cluster-wide, you need a ClusterRoleBinding instead.

Subjects come in three kinds. `ServiceAccount` needs a `name` and a `namespace`, and that namespace may differ from the binding's — a common way to let a controller in `kube-system` act in an application namespace. `User` and `Group` are strings validated by nothing; they are whatever your authentication layer asserts, so a typo produces a binding that silently matches nobody. For ServiceAccounts the corresponding user string is `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` and the group is `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>`.

`roleRef` is immutable. Changing which role a binding points at means deleting and recreating it — `kubectl apply` on a modified roleRef fails.
whenToUse: Giving a team's group edit rights in their own namespace
Granting an application's ServiceAccount the permissions it needs, and no more
Applying a shared ClusterRole such as view namespace by namespace
Letting a controller in another namespace operate on resources in this one

keyFields.description: Role or ClusterRole. Immutable.
Name of the role being granted.
Always rbac.authorization.k8s.io.
ServiceAccount, User or Group.
The subject's name. For User and Group this is an unvalidated string from your authenticator.
Required for ServiceAccount subjects, and may differ from the binding's namespace.

example:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: config-reader-binding
  namespace: default
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: backup-agent
    namespace: default
  - kind: User
    name: jane@example.com
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  - kind: Group
    name: developers
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: config-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
commonMistakes: Expecting a RoleBinding to a ClusterRole to grant cluster-wide permissions. It is still scoped to the binding's namespace.
Omitting namespace on a ServiceAccount subject. It does not default helpfully and the grant misses.
Editing roleRef on an existing binding. It is immutable — delete and recreate.
Misspelling a User or Group name. Nothing validates it, so the binding exists and grants nothing.
Adding apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io to a ServiceAccount subject. ServiceAccounts are in the core group, so the field is omitted for them.
kubectlTips: kubectl create rolebinding config-reader-binding --role=config-reader --serviceaccount=default:backup-agent --dry-run=client -o yaml  — get the shape right first time
kubectl auth can-i get configmaps --as=jane@example.com -n default  — test as a user
kubectl get rolebinding -A -o wide  — the SUBJECTS column makes it easy to audit who has what

summary: Grants a ClusterRole's permissions across every namespace and to cluster-scoped resources.
explanation:
A ClusterRoleBinding is the cluster-wide version of a RoleBinding. Its `roleRef` must be a ClusterRole — you cannot promote a namespaced Role this way — and the permissions apply everywhere: every existing namespace, every namespace created later, plus all cluster-scoped resources.

That last part is the risk. "Every namespace created later" means a ClusterRoleBinding written today silently covers next year's namespaces too. A binding granting Secret read access cluster-wide is a standing grant over every credential anyone will ever create. This is why the default advice is to reach for a RoleBinding first and only escalate when the workload genuinely needs cluster reach.

The canonical dangerous example is binding the `cluster-admin` ClusterRole to a ServiceAccount. That is complete control of the cluster, including the ability to create further bindings, which makes any compromise of that Pod a full cluster compromise. It shows up depressingly often in quick-start manifests.

Legitimate uses are real, though: monitoring agents that must read Pods everywhere, ingress controllers that watch Ingresses across all namespaces, cluster autoscalers that read Nodes. The test is whether the workload's job is genuinely cluster-wide. RBAC prevents privilege escalation: a subject can only create a binding granting permissions it already holds, unless it has the special `escalate` verb. That is why granting someone `create` on ClusterRoleBindings is effectively granting them everything they could ever bind.
whenToUse: Monitoring and logging agents that read resources in all namespaces
Ingress controllers, cert-manager and other cluster-wide operators
Granting real cluster administrators the cluster-admin role
Access to cluster-scoped resources such as Nodes and PersistentVolumes

keyFields.description: Must be ClusterRole. Immutable.
The ClusterRole being granted cluster-wide.
ServiceAccounts (with namespace), Users or Groups receiving the permissions.

example:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: node-reader-binding
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: monitoring-agent
    namespace: monitoring
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
commonMistakes: Binding cluster-admin to an application ServiceAccount to make an error go away — that hands the cluster to anything that compromises the Pod.
Using a ClusterRoleBinding when a RoleBinding in one namespace would do, quietly granting access to namespaces that do not exist yet.
Referencing a Role in roleRef. Only a ClusterRole is valid here.
Binding to the group system:authenticated, which includes every authenticated identity in the cluster.
Forgetting that granting create on clusterrolebindings is close to granting cluster-admin itself.
kubectlTips: kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o wide  — audit every cluster-wide grant, especially any pointing at cluster-admin
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name=="cluster-admin") | .metadata.name'  — find the dangerous ones
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:monitoring-agent  — confirm the effective permissions

summary: Asks the cluster to sign an X.509 certificate, which is how client certificates for users are issued.
explanation:
Kubernetes has no User objects, so authenticating a human means presenting a credential the API server trusts. One option is a client certificate signed by the cluster CA, and the CertificateSigningRequest API is how you get one without handling the CA key directly.

The flow has three steps. You generate a private key and a CSR locally, where the certificate's Common Name becomes the Kubernetes username and each Organization becomes a group. You submit the base64-encoded CSR in `spec.request`. Then someone with permission approves it (`kubectl certificate approve`), a signer issues the certificate, and it appears base64-encoded in `status.certificate`.

Approval and signing are deliberately separate. Approval is an RBAC-gated decision recorded on the object; signing is done by a controller watching for approved requests. `spec.signerName` picks which signer, and it is required. `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client` issues client certs for API authentication; `kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving` and `kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet` handle node certificates and are how kubelet TLS bootstrapping and rotation work.

The practical drawback is revocation: Kubernetes does not support certificate revocation lists. A leaked client certificate is valid until it expires, and the only real remedy is rotating the cluster CA. Keep `expirationSeconds` short, and prefer OIDC for human users in anything long-lived.
whenToUse: Issuing a client certificate for a human user in a small cluster
Understanding kubelet TLS bootstrapping and certificate rotation
Automated in-cluster certificate issuance by controllers with a custom signer
Not for serving certificates on applications — use cert-manager for those

keyFields.description: Base64-encoded PEM certificate signing request. The CN becomes the username and each O becomes a group.
Required. Which signer should issue it, e.g. kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client.
Key usages requested, such as client auth. Must match what the signer permits.
Requested lifetime. Signers may cap it; minimum is 600.
The signed certificate, base64-encoded, once approved and issued.
Approved, Denied or Failed.

example:
apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1
kind: CertificateSigningRequest
metadata:
  name: jane-client-cert
spec:
  request: 
  signerName: kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client
  expirationSeconds: 86400
  usages:
    - client auth
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a CSR is only a request. Until someone approves it, no certificate is issued.
Omitting spec.signerName. It is required in certificates.k8s.io/v1 and the object is rejected.
Expecting the certificate to grant permissions. It only authenticates; you still need a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding.
Including a newline when base64-encoding the CSR. Use base64 -w0 or the request will not parse.
Assuming a leaked certificate can be revoked. Kubernetes has no CRL support — short lifetimes are the only mitigation.
kubectlTips: kubectl get csr  — pending requests waiting for approval
kubectl certificate approve jane-client-cert  — approve one
kubectl get csr jane-client-cert -o jsonpath='{.status.certificate}' | base64 -d > jane.crt  — extract the signed certificate
kubectl config set-credentials jane --client-certificate=jane.crt --client-key=jane.key  — wire it into a kubeconfig

summary: A machine in the cluster that can run Pods — physical, virtual, or a cloud instance.
explanation:
A Node object is Kubernetes' record of a machine. It is unusual among API objects in that you rarely create it: the kubelet on each machine registers itself with the API server and keeps its own Node object updated. What you do edit is the parts that influence scheduling — labels, taints and `unschedulable`.

The Node's `status` carries the machine's `capacity` (total CPU, memory, pods and other resources) and `allocatable` (what remains for Pods after the kubelet and system reservations). The scheduler works from `allocatable` and from the sum of Pod resource *requests* already placed there, not from actual usage. A node can therefore be full from the scheduler's point of view while sitting almost idle, if Pods request far more than they use.

Health is reported through conditions. `Ready` is the one that matters most; `MemoryPressure`, `DiskPressure` and `PIDPressure` cause the kubelet to start evicting Pods. The node proves it is alive by renewing a Lease object in `kube-node-lease` every few seconds — cheaper than rewriting the whole Node object, which is what older versions did.

Taints are the node-side half of the scheduling contract: a taint repels Pods that lack a matching toleration. `NoSchedule` blocks new Pods, `PreferNoSchedule` is a soft version, and `NoExecute` additionally evicts Pods already running. Control-plane nodes carry a `NoSchedule` taint out of the box, which is why ordinary workloads do not land on them. Draining a node (`kubectl drain`) cordons it and evicts its Pods via the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. Deleting a Node object does not stop the machine — it just removes the record, and a running kubelet will re-register it.
whenToUse: Labelling nodes so workloads can target them: GPU, zone, instance type
Tainting nodes to reserve them for particular workloads
Cordoning and draining before maintenance or an upgrade
Reading capacity and conditions when Pods will not schedule

keyFields.description: Scheduling targets for nodeSelector and affinity. Standard ones include topology.kubernetes.io/zone and node.kubernetes.io/instance-type.
Repel Pods without a matching toleration. Effects: NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute.
True when cordoned; the scheduler places no new Pods, but existing ones keep running.
Pod IP range assigned to this node by the cluster's network.
Resources available to Pods after system reservations — what the scheduler actually budgets against.
Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, NetworkUnavailable.
Kubelet version, OS, kernel and container runtime — the first place to look for version skew.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Node
metadata:
  name: gpu-node-1
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: gpu-node-1
    node.kubernetes.io/instance-type: g4dn.xlarge
    topology.kubernetes.io/zone: us-east-1a
    hardware: gpu
spec:
  taints:
    - key: hardware
      value: gpu
      effect: NoSchedule
commonMistakes: Reading node CPU as usage. The scheduler counts requests, so a node can be unschedulable while its actual utilisation is low.
Deleting a Node object to remove a machine. The kubelet simply re-registers it; stop the kubelet or remove the instance.
Tainting a node with NoExecute without checking what is running. Pods without a matching toleration are evicted immediately.
Using kubectl delete pod instead of kubectl drain for maintenance, which ignores PodDisruptionBudgets.
Editing labels or taints directly in a managed node group. The cloud provider replaces the node and the change is lost — set them in the node group configuration.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe node gpu-node-1  — Allocated resources at the bottom shows request totals versus capacity
kubectl drain gpu-node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data  — safely empty a node before maintenance
kubectl uncordon gpu-node-1  — allow scheduling again
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints  — see every taint in the cluster
kubectl top nodes  — actual usage, as opposed to requests (needs metrics-server)

summary: A lightweight lock used for heartbeats and for electing a single active leader among replicas.
explanation:
A Lease is a tiny object with one job: record that some identity holds a claim, and until when. `holderIdentity` says who, `leaseDurationSeconds` says for how long, and `renewTime` is bumped by the holder to keep it. If the holder stops renewing, the lease is considered expired and another candidate can take it by writing its own identity.

That mechanism gives you leader election without any external coordination service. Every replica of a controller races to update the same Lease; the API server's optimistic concurrency (resourceVersion checks) guarantees exactly one write wins. The winner acts as leader and keeps renewing; the losers idle and watch. This is how `kube-controller-manager` and `kube-scheduler` run several replicas for availability while only one is active, and it is what the leader-election libraries in controller-runtime and client-go use under the hood.

The other use is node heartbeats. Every node renews a Lease in the `kube-node-lease` namespace every few seconds. Before this existed, nodes proved liveness by updating their whole Node object, which in a large cluster meant constant writes of a sizeable resource. A Lease is a few hundred bytes, so the same heartbeat costs a fraction as much etcd traffic.

You seldom write Leases directly — you configure a controller to use one. It is worth understanding because a stuck controller often traces back to a Lease held by a replica that died without releasing it, where nothing happens until the duration expires.
whenToUse: Leader election for a custom controller or operator with multiple replicas
Understanding how node heartbeats work when diagnosing NotReady nodes
Debugging why a controller with several replicas appears idle
Rarely authored by hand; configured through a controller's leader-election settings

keyFields.description: Who currently holds the lease, usually a Pod name or a generated identity.
How long the claim is valid without renewal.
Last renewal timestamp. A stale value means the holder has stopped.
When the current holder first took the lease.
How many times leadership has changed — a rising count means leaders are flapping.

example:
apiVersion: coordination.k8s.io/v1
kind: Lease
metadata:
  name: my-controller-leader
  namespace: default
spec:
  holderIdentity: my-controller-6b8f9d4c7-xk2p9
  leaseDurationSeconds: 15
  acquireTime: "2026-01-15T10:00:00.000000Z"
  renewTime: "2026-01-15T10:04:32.000000Z"
  leaseTransitions: 2
commonMistakes: Assuming a controller with 3 replicas does 3x the work. With leader election only one replica is active.
Setting leaseDurationSeconds very high, so failover after a leader crash takes that long.
Setting it very low, so a brief API server hiccup causes leadership to flap and controllers to restart their work.
Deleting a Lease to 'reset' a controller. Another replica grabs it immediately, which may not be what you wanted.
Forgetting to grant a custom controller create, get and update on leases in its namespace — leader election then fails silently at startup.
kubectlTips: kubectl get leases -n kube-system  — see which replica currently leads each control-plane component
kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease  — node heartbeats; a stale renewTime explains a NotReady node
kubectl get lease my-controller-leader -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}'  — identify the active replica

summary: A deprecated read-only view of control-plane component health; use component health endpoints instead.
explanation:
**Legacy and read-only.** ComponentStatus was an early attempt at a health summary for the control plane — scheduler, controller-manager and etcd. It was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.19 and has had no maintainer since; it is documented as likely to be removed.

It never worked well. The API server discovered components by connecting to hardcoded addresses, typically on localhost, which meant it only reported correctly on a single-node control plane. On any HA cluster, or any managed service where the control plane runs somewhere you cannot see, it reports `Unhealthy` or empty results for perfectly healthy components. This is a common false alarm for people learning on managed clusters.

Unlike almost every other object here, you do not author one. There is no `spec`; the object is synthesised on read from the API server's probe results and exists only as a query response. The example below shows what the API returns, not something to apply.

The replacements are the health endpoints on each component: `/healthz`, `/livez` and `/readyz` on the API server (`/readyz?verbose` breaks the result down by individual check), and the components' own metrics endpoints. For anything real, Prometheus scraping those endpoints is the answer.
whenToUse: Nothing new — it is deprecated and unreliable
Recognising it in old runbooks and tutorials so you know to ignore the output
Use kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose' instead

keyFields.description: Always Healthy. Top-level; the object has no spec.
True, False or Unknown. Frequently wrong on HA and managed clusters.
Raw probe output, such as the string 'ok' from a component's health endpoint.

example:
# Read-only: this is what the API returns, not a manifest you apply.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ComponentStatus
metadata:
  name: scheduler
conditions:
  - type: Healthy
    status: "True"
    message: ok
commonMistakes: Alerting on ComponentStatus output. On managed or HA clusters it reports Unhealthy for components that are fine.
Trying to create or edit one. It is synthesised on read and has no spec.
Assuming an empty result means the control plane is broken. On EKS, GKE and AKS the control plane simply is not reachable this way.
Using it in new monitoring. Scrape /readyz and component metrics endpoints instead.
kubectlTips: kubectl get --raw '/readyz?verbose'  — the modern replacement, with a line per health check
kubectl get --raw '/livez?verbose'  — liveness rather than readiness
kubectl get componentstatuses  — only to confirm the deprecated view is as unhelpful as expected

summary: Registers an additional API group/version, either built in or served by an external extension server.
explanation:
The Kubernetes API server can delegate parts of the API surface to other servers. An APIService is the routing entry that makes that happen: it says "requests for group `metrics.k8s.io`, version `v1beta1` should be proxied to this Service". This is API aggregation, and it is one of the two ways to extend the API — the other being CustomResourceDefinitions.

The difference matters. A CRD stores your objects in etcd and the main API server handles them; you write no server code. An aggregated APIService points at a server you run, which can compute responses on the fly, store data elsewhere, or serve things that are not really objects at all. The canonical example is metrics-server: `kubectl top` works because an APIService routes `metrics.k8s.io` to it, and the metrics are computed live rather than stored.

Each APIService names its `group` and `version`, plus a `service` reference and a `caBundle` used to verify the extension server's TLS certificate. Local built-in groups are registered with no service reference and `spec.service: null`. `groupPriorityMinimum` and `versionPriority` control ordering when several APIServices could serve overlapping resources, which affects what `kubectl api-resources` shows first.

APIServices are a classic source of cluster-wide breakage. If the backing Service is down, requests to that group fail — and because discovery enumerates all groups, a single broken APIService can make `kubectl get all` hang or error, and can block namespace deletion entirely. Checking `kubectl get apiservices` for anything not `True` is a standard first move when a cluster behaves strangely.
whenToUse: Installing metrics-server, custom metrics adapters or other aggregated API servers
Serving an API whose responses are computed rather than stored
Diagnosing discovery failures, hanging kubectl commands or stuck namespace deletion
Created by extension components' install manifests rather than by hand

keyFields.description: API group being registered, e.g. metrics.k8s.io.
Version within that group.
Service backing the extension server. Null for locally served built-in groups.
Base64 CA bundle used to verify the extension server's certificate.
Skip certificate verification. Convenient, insecure, and mutually exclusive with caBundle.
Group ordering across APIServices; higher wins.
Ordering of versions within the group.
Available=True means the backing server is reachable. Anything else breaks discovery.

example:
apiVersion: apiregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: APIService
metadata:
  name: v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
spec:
  group: metrics.k8s.io
  version: v1beta1
  groupPriorityMinimum: 100
  versionPriority: 100
  insecureSkipTLSVerify: true
  service:
    name: metrics-server
    namespace: kube-system
    port: 443
commonMistakes: Naming the object arbitrarily. It must be exactly <version>.<group>, e.g. v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io.
Leaving a broken APIService in place. Discovery calls fail and unrelated commands like kubectl get all start hanging.
Deleting an extension's Deployment but not its APIService, which then blocks namespace deletion on failed discovery.
Setting both caBundle and insecureSkipTLSVerify. They are mutually exclusive.
Expecting an APIService to store objects. It only routes; the backing server decides what to do with them.
kubectlTips: kubectl get apiservices  — anything with AVAILABLE False is a live problem
kubectl get apiservices | grep -v True  — the one-liner for diagnosing weird cluster-wide failures
kubectl describe apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io  — the failure reason for an unavailable extension

summary: Classifies incoming API requests into priority levels so one noisy client cannot starve the API server.
explanation:
API Priority and Fairness is the API server's built-in protection against overload. Without it, a single controller in a hot loop could consume all request capacity and effectively take the control plane down for everyone. FlowSchema is the classification half of the system.

Each FlowSchema matches requests by subject (users, groups, ServiceAccounts) and by what they are doing (`resourceRules` for object access, `nonResourceRules` for paths like `/healthz`). Matching requests are assigned to the PriorityLevelConfiguration named in `spec.priorityLevelConfiguration`, which is where the actual concurrency budget lives.

`matchingPrecedence` orders the schemas — lower numbers are evaluated first, and the first match wins. Built-in schemas occupy well-known precedences, so custom ones are usually given a value between them. `distinguisherMethod` decides how requests within a priority level are subdivided into flows for fair queuing: `ByUser` gives each user their own queue, `ByNamespace` gives each namespace one, and omitting it puts everything in a single flow. This is what stops one busy namespace from monopolising a shared priority level.

When a level is saturated, requests queue and eventually receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Well-behaved clients back off. The practical signal that this is happening is a rise in 429s and in the `apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total` metric — and the fix is usually to fix the client, not to raise the limits.
whenToUse: Protecting the API server from a specific noisy controller or CI system
Guaranteeing capacity for critical traffic such as leader election and node heartbeats
Diagnosing 429 responses from the API server
Rarely needed — the built-in schemas cover most clusters well

keyFields.description: Which PriorityLevelConfiguration handles matching requests.
Evaluation order, 1 to 10000. Lower is checked first; first match wins.
ByUser or ByNamespace — how requests are split into fair-queued flows. Omit for a single flow.
Who the rule matches: User, Group or ServiceAccount.
Verbs, API groups, resources and namespaces this rule covers.
Non-resource URL paths this rule covers.

example:
apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1
kind: FlowSchema
metadata:
  name: batch-jobs-low-priority
spec:
  priorityLevelConfiguration:
    name: batch-low
  matchingPrecedence: 900
  distinguisherMethod:
    type: ByUser
  rules:
    - subjects:
        - kind: ServiceAccount
          serviceAccount:
            name: batch-runner
            namespace: batch
      resourceRules:
        - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
          apiGroups: ["", "batch"]
          resources: ["pods", "jobs"]
          namespaces: ["batch"]
commonMistakes: Referencing a PriorityLevelConfiguration that does not exist. The schema is created but never becomes effective.
Choosing a matchingPrecedence that collides with a built-in schema, so requests are classified somewhere unexpected.
Raising concurrency limits to make 429s go away, instead of fixing the client that is hammering the API.
Forgetting namespaces on a resourceRule, so it matches far more traffic than intended.
Copying flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta2 or v1beta3 examples. The API reached v1 in Kubernetes 1.29.
kubectlTips: kubectl get flowschemas  — built-in schemas listed in precedence order
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected  — confirm requests are actually being rejected
kubectl get flowschema -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PL:.spec.priorityLevelConfiguration.name,PRECEDENCE:.spec.matchingPrecedence  — see the mapping at a glance

summary: Defines how much concurrent API server capacity a class of requests may use, and what happens when it is exceeded.
explanation:
If FlowSchema decides which bucket a request goes into, PriorityLevelConfiguration decides how big that bucket is. Together they form API Priority and Fairness. `spec.type` is either `Exempt` or `Limited`. `Exempt` means requests bypass throttling entirely — reserved for traffic that must never be delayed, such as requests from cluster administrators and some system components. `Limited` means the level gets a share of the API server's total concurrency budget.

That share is set by `nominalConcurrencyShares`, and it is a weight, not a request count. Each Limited level's seats are its shares divided by the sum of all levels' shares, multiplied by the server's total concurrency. Adding a new level therefore dilutes every existing one, which is why creating custom levels casually is discouraged. (In the older `v1beta2` API this field was called `assuredConcurrencyShares`; it was renamed when the API went to v1 in Kubernetes 1.29.)

`limitResponse` says what happens when the seats are full. `Reject` returns HTTP 429 immediately. `Queue` holds requests in fair queues first, with `queues` setting how many, `queueLengthLimit` how deep each may get, and `handSize` how many queues a given flow is hashed across — shuffle sharding, so that one heavy flow rarely collides with the same neighbours in every queue.

`lendablePercent` and `borrowingLimitPercent` let idle levels lend capacity to busy ones, so reserved-but-unused seats are not simply wasted.
whenToUse: Reserving API server capacity for critical traffic
Capping a specific class of requests that keeps overwhelming the control plane
Understanding why the API server returns 429 under load
Usually left at the built-in defaults, which are well tuned

keyFields.description: Exempt (never throttled) or Limited (gets a concurrency share).
Weight, not an absolute count. Seats are shares divided by the total of all levels' shares.
Queue or Reject when the level is saturated.
Number of queues for fair sharing within the level.
How many queues each flow is hashed across — the shuffle-sharding parameter.
Maximum requests held per queue before rejection.
Portion of this level's seats other levels may borrow when idle.

example:
apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityLevelConfiguration
metadata:
  name: batch-low
spec:
  type: Limited
  limited:
    nominalConcurrencyShares: 10
    lendablePercent: 50
    limitResponse:
      type: Queue
      queuing:
        queues: 32
        handSize: 6
        queueLengthLimit: 50
commonMistakes: Reading nominalConcurrencyShares as a number of requests. It is a relative weight against every other level.
Creating many custom levels, which dilutes the shares of the built-in ones and can starve system traffic.
Setting handSize larger than queues, which is invalid and rejected.
Using assuredConcurrencyShares, the pre-v1 field name. In flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1 it is nominalConcurrencyShares.
Choosing Reject for user-facing traffic when Queue would have smoothed a brief burst.
kubectlTips: kubectl get prioritylevelconfigurations  — the built-in levels and their types
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_flowcontrol_request_concurrency_limit  — the seats each level actually received
kubectl describe prioritylevelconfiguration batch-low  — verify queuing parameters after a change

summary: Caps the total amount of CPU, memory, storage or object count a namespace may consume.
explanation:
A ResourceQuota is a budget for a namespace. It constrains aggregate consumption — the sum of all Pods' CPU requests, total memory limits, number of Services, number of PVCs — so one team cannot take the whole cluster.

Enforcement happens at admission time, when an object is created. If creating a Pod would push the namespace over its quota, the API server rejects it with a 403 and a message naming the exceeded resource. Importantly, the rejection lands on whatever tried to create the object, so a Deployment that hits quota does not fail visibly itself — its ReplicaSet does, and the error only shows up in `kubectl describe replicaset` events. This is a frequent source of "my Deployment says 3 replicas but only 1 Pod exists".

The compute quota has a sharp side effect. If a quota specifies `requests.cpu` or `limits.memory`, then every Pod created in that namespace must set those values explicitly — otherwise the quota system cannot account for it and the Pod is refused. In practice you pair every compute ResourceQuota with a LimitRange that supplies defaults, or every existing manifest without resources suddenly breaks.

Object counts are written as `count/<resource>.<group>` — `count/deployments.apps`, `count/services`. This is how you stop runaway controllers creating thousands of objects. A handful of resources also have legacy shorthand names such as `pods`, `services` and `persistentvolumeclaims`. `scopes` and `scopeSelector` narrow a quota to a subset of Pods — `BestEffort` Pods only, terminating Pods only, or Pods of a given PriorityClass. That last one is how you reserve capacity for high-priority workloads while capping low-priority ones.
whenToUse: Multi-tenant clusters where teams share capacity
Preventing one namespace from consuming the whole cluster
Limiting expensive objects such as LoadBalancer Services or PVCs
Reserving capacity by PriorityClass using scopeSelector

keyFields.description: Total CPU requests allowed across all Pods in the namespace.
Total memory limits allowed across all Pods.
Maximum number of non-terminal Pods.
Total storage requested across all PVCs.
Object-count quota; the count/<resource>.<group> form works for any resource.
Terminating, NotTerminating, BestEffort, NotBestEffort, PriorityClass.
Finer scoping, e.g. only Pods with a particular PriorityClass.
Current consumption against each limit — the field to read when something is being rejected.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-quota
  namespace: production
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 40Gi
    limits.cpu: "40"
    limits.memory: 80Gi
    pods: "100"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "20"
    requests.storage: 500Gi
    services.loadbalancers: "2"
    count/deployments.apps: "50"
commonMistakes: Creating a compute quota without a matching LimitRange. Every Pod without explicit resources is then rejected.
Looking for the error on the Deployment. Quota rejections appear on the ReplicaSet's events, not the Deployment's.
Assuming a quota reduces existing usage. It only blocks new objects; workloads already over the limit keep running.
Forgetting that limits.memory quota counts limits, so Pods with no limit set are unaccounted and refused.
Writing count/deployments instead of count/deployments.apps and having the quota match nothing.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe quota -n production  — a used-versus-hard table, the fastest way to see what is exhausted
kubectl get resourcequota -n production -o yaml  — status.used in full detail
kubectl describe rs <name> -n production  — where quota rejection events actually surface

summary: Sets default, minimum and maximum CPU and memory for containers in a namespace.
explanation:
Where a ResourceQuota caps the namespace total, a LimitRange governs individual objects. It does two jobs: injecting defaults into containers that specify none, and rejecting containers whose values fall outside allowed bounds.

The defaulting behaviour is what makes it essential alongside quotas. `defaultRequest` supplies `resources.requests` and `default` supplies `resources.limits` for any container that omits them, applied by an admission controller at creation time. Without this, a namespace with a compute ResourceQuota rejects every Pod that does not spell out its resources — which is most existing manifests.

Defaults are stamped onto the Pod at admission. Change the LimitRange and running Pods keep their old values; only newly created Pods pick up the new defaults. `min` and `max` set bounds, and a container outside them is refused with a clear error. `maxLimitRequestRatio` is the subtle one: it caps how far a limit may exceed its request. A ratio of 4 means a container requesting 250m CPU cannot have a limit above 1. This limits overcommitment, since a Pod requesting little but permitted a lot is exactly what causes node-level contention.

`type` selects what a limit entry applies to: `Container` (per container), `Pod` (the sum across all containers in a Pod) and `PersistentVolumeClaim` (storage size bounds). Only `Container` entries can carry defaults.
whenToUse: Any namespace with a compute ResourceQuota — to supply the required defaults
Stopping a single Pod from requesting an entire node
Giving sensible baseline resources to teams who omit them
Bounding PVC sizes so nobody provisions a 10Ti disk by accident

keyFields.description: Container, Pod or PersistentVolumeClaim.
Default resources.limits for containers that specify none.
Default resources.requests for containers that specify none.
Minimum allowed value; smaller requests are rejected.
Maximum allowed value; larger limits are rejected.
Cap on limit divided by request, restricting overcommitment.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: production
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: 500m
        memory: 512Mi
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      min:
        cpu: 10m
        memory: 32Mi
      max:
        cpu: "4"
        memory: 8Gi
      maxLimitRequestRatio:
        cpu: "10"
    - type: PersistentVolumeClaim
      min:
        storage: 1Gi
      max:
        storage: 500Gi
commonMistakes: Expecting a changed LimitRange to update running Pods. Defaults are applied at creation only.
Setting min above the defaultRequest, so every defaulted Pod is immediately rejected as too small.
Assuming a LimitRange caps namespace totals. That is a ResourceQuota; this bounds individual containers.
Setting defaults so high that a few Pods exhaust the namespace quota.
Putting default or defaultRequest on a Pod-type or PVC-type entry, where they are not supported.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe limitrange defaults -n production  — a readable table of defaults and bounds
kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources}'  — see what was actually injected
kubectl get limitrange -A  — find namespaces with no defaults configured

summary: Guarantees a minimum number of Pods stay running during voluntary disruptions like node drains.
explanation:
Kubernetes distinguishes two kinds of disruption. Involuntary ones — a node crashing, hardware failing, an OOM kill — cannot be negotiated. Voluntary ones — draining a node for an upgrade, a cluster autoscaler removing an underused node — go through the Eviction API, and that is where a PodDisruptionBudget applies.

The budget states how much simultaneous disruption is acceptable, using either `minAvailable` (at least this many must stay up) or `maxUnavailable` (at most this many may be down), each as a count or a percentage. When something calls the Eviction API, the API server checks the budget: if evicting the Pod would violate it, the eviction is refused with a 429 and the caller retries. This is what makes `kubectl drain` on a three-node cluster take its time rather than removing all replicas of a service at once.

A PDB constrains evictions only. It does not stop `kubectl delete pod`, and it cannot prevent a node from failing. It is a coordination mechanism between whoever is doing maintenance and whoever owns the workload — not a durability guarantee. The classic self-inflicted wound is a budget the workload can never satisfy: `minAvailable: 1` on a single-replica Deployment. Evicting the only Pod would leave zero available, so every eviction is refused and node drains hang forever. The rule of thumb is that a PDB needs at least one more replica than the budget requires.

`unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy` addresses a related deadlock: by default, Pods that are already unhealthy still count against the budget, so a workload stuck in CrashLoopBackOff can block a drain indefinitely. Setting it to `AlwaysAllow` lets unready Pods be evicted regardless.
whenToUse: Any multi-replica service that should stay available during cluster upgrades
Quorum systems where losing two of three members is fatal
Clusters running a node autoscaler that removes nodes automatically
Not on single-replica workloads unless you deliberately want drains to block

keyFields.description: Minimum Pods that must remain available. Count or percentage. Mutually exclusive with maxUnavailable.
Maximum Pods that may be unavailable at once. Often the clearer choice with an autoscaled workload.
Which Pods the budget covers. Must match the workload's Pod labels.
IfHealthyBudget (default) or AlwaysAllow, which permits evicting unready Pods so a crashing workload cannot block drains.
How many evictions are permitted right now. A persistent 0 means drains will hang.

example:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
  namespace: production
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
commonMistakes: minAvailable: 1 on a single-replica Deployment. Nothing can ever be evicted and node drains hang indefinitely.
Setting minAvailable equal to spec.replicas, which allows zero disruption and blocks every upgrade.
Expecting a PDB to protect against node failure. It only governs voluntary evictions.
A selector that does not match the workload's Pods, producing a budget that silently protects nothing.
Forgetting that a CrashLoopBackOff Pod counts as unavailable, blocking drains until unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy is set to AlwaysAllow.
kubectlTips: kubectl get pdb -A  — the ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS column; any persistent 0 is a future stuck drain
kubectl describe pdb web-pdb -n production  — shows expected versus current healthy Pods
kubectl drain <node> --dry-run=server  — see which PDBs would block a drain before you start

summary: Automatically adds or removes Pod replicas based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.
explanation:
An HPA changes the replica count of a Deployment, StatefulSet or any resource with a `scale` subresource. Every 15 seconds by default it reads the current metric value and computes a target: `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric)`. If Pods average 80% CPU against a 50% target, that arithmetic says scale from 3 to 5.

Metrics come from the metrics APIs, not from the Pods directly, so you must have metrics-server installed for CPU and memory targets — without it the HPA reports `unknown` and does nothing. Custom and external metrics require an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter or KEDA registering `custom.metrics.k8s.io` or `external.metrics.k8s.io`.

CPU utilisation targets are percentages of the Pod's CPU **request**, not of the node or of any limit. A Pod requesting 100m and using 80m is at 80%. This means an HPA cannot work on a Pod with no CPU request — a very common misconfiguration, and the reason so many HPAs sit at `<unknown>/50%`. With multiple metrics in `spec.metrics`, the HPA computes a desired count for each and takes the largest, so it scales up for whichever resource is most stressed.

Scaling down is deliberately cautious. `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` (300 by default) makes the controller use the highest recommendation from the last five minutes, so a brief traffic dip does not immediately remove capacity. Scale-up has a zero-second window by default so it can respond quickly. Both directions can be shaped further with `policies` limiting how many Pods or what percentage may change per period. Because the HPA owns `spec.replicas`, leaving that field in a Deployment managed by GitOps causes a tug-of-war: the HPA scales up, the sync reverts it, repeatedly. Omit `replicas` from the manifest.
whenToUse: Web services and APIs with variable traffic
Queue consumers scaled on queue depth via an external metric
Any stateless workload where more replicas genuinely means more throughput
Not for workloads bounded by a database or an external rate limit — more replicas will not help

keyFields.description: The workload to scale, by apiVersion, kind and name.
Floor for scaling. Defaults to 1.
Ceiling. Required.
Resource, Pods, Object, External or ContainerResource.
Target percentage of the Pods' resource requests.
Look-back window that damps scale-down. Default 300.
Rate limits on scale-up, e.g. at most 100% or 4 Pods per 60 seconds.
What the HPA is actually reading. <unknown> here means the metrics pipeline is broken.

example:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: production
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: memory
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 80
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100
          periodSeconds: 60
        - type: Pods
          value: 4
          periodSeconds: 60
      selectPolicy: Max
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 25
          periodSeconds: 60
commonMistakes: No CPU request on the containers. Utilisation is a percentage of the request, so with none the HPA reports <unknown> and never scales.
No metrics-server installed. The HPA exists, reads nothing, and does nothing.
Keeping spec.replicas in a Deployment that an HPA also manages, so GitOps and the HPA fight and replicas oscillate.
Using autoscaling/v1, which only supports CPU and none of the behavior tuning.
Running an HPA and a VPA in Auto mode on the same CPU metric — they feed each other and the workload thrashes.
Setting minReplicas: 1 for a service that must stay available during node drains, leaving the PDB unable to allow any disruption.
kubectlTips: kubectl get hpa  — TARGETS shows current versus target; <unknown> means the metrics pipeline is broken
kubectl describe hpa web  — Conditions and Events explain exactly why it is not scaling
kubectl top pods  — confirm metrics-server is actually returning data
kubectl autoscale deploy/web --min=3 --max=20 --cpu-percent=70  — create a simple one imperatively

summary: Recommends or automatically sets CPU and memory requests for Pods based on observed usage.
explanation:
**Not part of core Kubernetes.** The VerticalPodAutoscaler is a separate project under kubernetes/autoscaler, installed as CRDs plus three components: a recommender, an updater and an admission controller. `kubectl get vpa` fails on a cluster where it has not been installed. Some managed platforms offer it as an add-on.

Where an HPA changes how many Pods you run, a VPA changes how big each one is. The recommender watches actual CPU and memory consumption over time, builds a usage histogram per container, and publishes recommended requests in `status.recommendation` — a lower bound, a target, and an upper bound. This solves a real problem: most resource requests are guesses, and guessing high wastes cluster capacity while guessing low causes throttling and OOM kills.

`updatePolicy.updateMode` decides what happens with those numbers. `Off` only records recommendations, which is the safest and most common mode — you read them and update your manifests yourself. `Initial` applies them to new Pods only. `Auto` and `Recreate` evict running Pods so they restart with the new requests, because for most of the VPA's history request changes required recreating the Pod.

That eviction behaviour is the main operational caveat: in `Auto` mode your Pods get restarted, at times the VPA chooses. (Kubernetes 1.33 added in-place Pod resizing as a beta feature, which newer VPA versions can use to reduce restarts, but do not assume it is active on your cluster.) Do not run a VPA and an HPA against the same resource metric. The HPA scales out when CPU utilisation rises; the VPA raises the CPU request, which lowers measured utilisation; the HPA then scales back in. The two chase each other. Combining them is only safe when the HPA is driven by a custom or external metric that the VPA does not influence.
whenToUse: Discovering correct requests for a workload nobody sized properly
Workloads that cannot scale horizontally — single-writer databases, some batch jobs
Continuous rightsizing to reduce cluster cost
In Off mode as a recommendation engine, which is where most teams should start

keyFields.description: The workload to size, by apiVersion, kind and name.
Off, Initial, Recreate or Auto. Off only recommends.
Floor for recommendations, per container.
Ceiling, so a recommendation never exceeds what a node can fit.
Which resources to manage, typically cpu and memory.
Auto or Off per container — use Off to exclude a sidecar.
target, lowerBound, upperBound and uncappedTarget per container.

example:
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: production
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: web
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
      - containerName: "nginx"
        controlledResources: ["cpu", "memory"]
        minAllowed:
          cpu: 50m
          memory: 64Mi
        maxAllowed:
          cpu: "2"
          memory: 4Gi
      - containerName: "istio-proxy"
        mode: "Off"
commonMistakes: Expecting it to exist on a stock cluster. The VPA must be installed separately; it is not a core API.
Running VPA in Auto mode alongside a CPU-based HPA on the same workload, so the two autoscalers oscillate against each other.
Being surprised by restarts in Auto mode. The updater evicts Pods to apply new requests.
Omitting maxAllowed, letting a recommendation exceed any node's capacity and leaving Pods unschedulable.
Using it on a workload with too little history — early recommendations from a short window are unreliable.
kubectlTips: kubectl describe vpa web -n production  — the recommendation block is the useful output even in Off mode
kubectl get vpa -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,MODE:.spec.updatePolicy.updateMode  — find any VPA quietly running in Auto
kubectl get crd | grep autoscaling.k8s.io  — confirm the VPA is installed at all

summary: Names a scheduling priority so important Pods can preempt less important ones when the cluster is full.
explanation:
A PriorityClass maps a name to an integer `value`. Pods reference the name in `spec.priorityClassName`, and the admission controller copies the number into `spec.priority`. Higher numbers mean higher priority.

Priority does two things. In the scheduling queue, higher-priority pending Pods are considered first, so they get the next free slot. And if no node can fit a high-priority Pod, the scheduler may **preempt**: it looks for a node where evicting one or more lower-priority Pods would make room, and deletes them. Preemption respects PodDisruptionBudgets on a best-effort basis only — it will violate a PDB rather than leave a high-priority Pod pending forever.

Evicted Pods are not moved; they are deleted, and their controllers create replacements that go back through scheduling. So a low-priority Deployment can lose Pods at any moment when the cluster fills. Preemption is a real, disruptive mechanism, not just queue ordering. Set `preemptionPolicy: Never` for a Pod that should jump the queue but never evict anything — the right setting for important-but-not-urgent batch work.

Like StorageClass, this object has no `spec`: `value`, `globalDefault`, `description` and `preemptionPolicy` are top-level fields. Two built-in classes exist for control-plane components: `system-cluster-critical` (2000000000) and `system-node-critical` (2000001000). Do not use them for applications — a misbehaving app at node-critical priority can evict the components that keep the node alive. `globalDefault: true` applies a class to every Pod that names none. Only one class may set it, and it changes the meaning of every existing unpriorized Pod in the cluster, so it deserves care.
whenToUse: Guaranteeing production workloads win over batch jobs when nodes are full
Marking cluster infrastructure so it is never evicted by application load
Running low-priority preemptible work that soaks up spare capacity
Reserving capacity by combining a PriorityClass with a ResourceQuota scopeSelector

keyFields.description: Integer priority; higher wins. Top-level field, not under spec.
Apply to Pods that specify no class. At most one PriorityClass may set this.
PreemptLowerPriority (default) or Never, which orders the queue without evicting anything.
Human-readable note explaining when to use the class.

example:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: production-critical
value: 1000000
globalDefault: false
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority
description: "Customer-facing production workloads. May preempt batch and dev workloads."
commonMistakes: Wrapping the fields in a spec block. PriorityClass has no spec.
Using system-node-critical for an application, letting it evict components the node depends on.
Assuming preemption always honours PodDisruptionBudgets. PDBs are best-effort during preemption.
Setting globalDefault on a second class — only one is allowed and the behaviour of existing Pods changes underneath you.
Expecting preempted Pods to be rescheduled elsewhere automatically. They are deleted; their controller must recreate them.
