kubectlTips: kubectl get priorityclass  — the values in use, including the two built-in system classes
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PRIORITY:.spec.priority  — see effective priorities
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Preempted  — find what has actually been evicted by preemption

summary: The Pod-side use of a PriorityClass: the field that decides scheduling order and eviction risk.
explanation:
**Conceptual entry — there is no PodPriority object.** Pod priority is the effect of two fields on a Pod: `spec.priorityClassName`, which you set, and `spec.priority`, the integer that the admission controller fills in from the named PriorityClass. This entry exists because the behaviour is significant enough to understand on its own, separately from the PriorityClass that defines it.

The number matters in three places. The scheduler sorts its pending queue by priority, so higher-priority Pods are placed first. When nothing fits, the scheduler may preempt lower-priority Pods to make room. And when a node runs out of memory or disk, the kubelet uses priority alongside QoS class to decide the eviction order.

QoS class is a related but distinct mechanism, derived from resource settings rather than priority. `Guaranteed` means every container has limits equal to requests; `Burstable` means requests are set and lower than limits; `BestEffort` means nothing is set. Under node pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable exceeding requests, then Guaranteed — and within a class, lower priority goes first. So a high-priority BestEffort Pod is still evicted before a low-priority Guaranteed one under memory pressure. Priority governs scheduling; QoS governs node-pressure eviction. Both are worth setting deliberately.

`spec.priority` is not something you set yourself: the API server overwrites it from the class. And `priorityClassName` is immutable on an existing Pod, so changing a workload's priority means a new Pod, which for a Deployment means a rollout.
whenToUse: Marking which workloads should survive when the cluster runs out of room
Understanding why a Pod was evicted or preempted
Pairing with QoS class — set requests equal to limits for Pods that must not be evicted
Set the class name on the Pod template; never set spec.priority directly

keyFields.description: Name of the PriorityClass to apply. The field you actually set. Immutable after Pod creation.
Integer copied from the class by admission control. Read-only in practice.
Inherited from the class; can be overridden per Pod to stop it preempting others.
Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort — derived from requests and limits, and the primary factor in node-pressure eviction.

example:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: production
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout
    spec:
      priorityClassName: production-critical
      containers:
        - name: checkout
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
commonMistakes: Setting spec.priority directly. It is overwritten from the PriorityClass at admission.
Naming a PriorityClass that does not exist. The Pod is rejected at admission with a clear error.
Assuming high priority protects against node-pressure eviction. A BestEffort Pod is evicted first no matter its priority — set requests and limits too.
Trying to change priorityClassName on a running Pod. It is immutable; recreate the Pod.
Giving everything high priority, which makes priority meaningless again.
kubectlTips: kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PRIORITY:.spec.priority,QOS:.status.qosClass  — the two fields that decide eviction order
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -i priority  — confirm what was actually applied
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Evicted  — see node-pressure evictions

summary: Lets a Pod choose which container runtime it runs under, such as a sandboxed or VM-isolated one.
explanation:
Most clusters run every container under one runtime, typically containerd or CRI-O with runc. Some workloads want stronger isolation than a shared kernel provides — untrusted code, multi-tenant functions, anything handling hostile input. RuntimeClass is how a Pod asks for a different runtime.

The object maps a friendly name to a `handler` string. That handler must be configured in the CRI runtime's own config on each node — for containerd, an entry under `plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes`. Kubernetes does not install runtimes; it only routes to handlers that already exist. A Pod referencing a RuntimeClass whose handler is missing on its node fails to start with a runtime error.

Common handlers are `runc` (the default, shared kernel), `runsc` for gVisor (a user-space kernel intercepting syscalls), and `kata` for Kata Containers (a lightweight VM per Pod). The stronger the isolation, the higher the startup and syscall overhead — a real trade-off, not a free upgrade. Because alternative runtimes usually exist on only some nodes, `scheduling.nodeSelector` constrains Pods using the class to nodes that have it, and `scheduling.tolerations` are added automatically so those nodes can be tainted against everything else. This is what makes a mixed-runtime cluster workable.

`overhead.podFixed` declares the extra CPU and memory the runtime itself consumes per Pod — meaningful for a VM-based runtime. The scheduler and node accounting include it, so a Kata Pod correctly counts against node capacity for more than just its containers. Like StorageClass and PriorityClass, RuntimeClass has no `spec`: `handler`, `scheduling` and `overhead` are top-level fields.
whenToUse: Running untrusted or customer-supplied code with kernel-level isolation
Multi-tenant platforms where a container escape must not reach other tenants
Mixed Windows and Linux clusters selecting the right runtime
Not needed at all if every workload is trusted and one runtime suffices

keyFields.description: CRI handler name, configured on the node's container runtime. Top-level field; required and immutable.
Restricts Pods using this class to nodes where the handler exists.
Tolerations automatically added to Pods using this class.
Per-Pod resource overhead of the runtime, counted by the scheduler and by node accounting.

example:
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    sandbox-runtime: "true"
  tolerations:
    - key: sandbox-runtime
      operator: Equal
      value: "true"
      effect: NoSchedule
overhead:
  podFixed:
    cpu: 50m
    memory: 64Mi
commonMistakes: Creating a RuntimeClass without installing the runtime on any node. Pods using it fail with a handler-not-found error at container creation.
Wrapping handler and scheduling in a spec block. This object has no spec.
Assuming a sandboxed runtime is a drop-in replacement. gVisor intercepts syscalls and some workloads are markedly slower or unsupported.
Forgetting overhead, so the scheduler underestimates what a VM-based Pod costs and overpacks nodes.
Expecting RuntimeClass to enforce security policy. It selects a runtime; policy enforcement is Pod Security Admission's job.
kubectlTips: kubectl get runtimeclass  — which runtimes the cluster offers
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RUNTIME:.spec.runtimeClassName  — see which Pods use a non-default runtime
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -i runtime  — the container runtime version actually present

summary: Enforces rules on objects at admission time using CEL expressions, with no webhook server to run.
explanation:
Before this existed, enforcing a rule like "every Deployment must set resource limits" meant running an admission webhook: a Deployment, a Service, a TLS certificate, and a network round trip on every matching API request — plus the risk that if your webhook is down, the cluster stops accepting objects.

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy moves that logic into the API server. You write expressions in CEL (Common Expression Language), a small, safe, non-Turing-complete language, and the API server evaluates them in-process. No server, no certificates, no latency, no availability risk. It reached GA in Kubernetes 1.30.

The design deliberately separates definition from application. The policy holds the rules — what to match (`matchConstraints`) and what to check (`validations`, each with an `expression` that must evaluate to true). A separate ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding says where the policy applies and how strictly. That split lets one policy be enforced in production and merely audited in staging.

Inside an expression, `object` is the incoming object, `oldObject` the existing one on updates, `request` the admission metadata, and `params` an optional configuration object supplied by the binding. `variables` let you name a sub-expression and reuse it, which keeps complex rules readable. It validates only. It cannot modify objects — that is what mutating webhooks, and the newer MutatingAdmissionPolicy, are for. And CEL has no I/O: a policy cannot call out to another service or look up other objects in the cluster, so cross-object rules still need a webhook.
whenToUse: Requiring resource limits, probes or specific labels on workloads
Blocking the :latest image tag or images from untrusted registries
Replacing simple OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno rules with a built-in mechanism
Not for rules needing external data or object mutation — those still need a webhook

keyFields.description: Which API groups, versions, resources and operations the policy inspects.
CEL expression that must be true for the request to be admitted.
Error text returned when the expression fails.
CEL expression producing a dynamic error message.
Fail (default) or Ignore, when the expression itself errors.
Named sub-expressions reusable across validations as variables.<name>.
CEL preconditions that narrow which requests are evaluated at all.
Type of configuration object a binding may supply as params.

example:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets", "daemonsets"]
  variables:
    - name: containers
      expression: "object.spec.template.spec.containers"
  validations:
    - expression: "variables.containers.all(c, has(c.resources) && has(c.resources.limits) && 'memory' in c.resources.limits)"
      message: "every container must set a memory limit"
    - expression: "variables.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))"
      message: "the :latest image tag is not allowed"
commonMistakes: Creating the policy and expecting it to do something. Nothing is enforced until a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding exists.
Accessing an optional field directly instead of guarding with has(). The expression errors, and under failurePolicy: Fail that blocks the request.
Trying to mutate the object. This API only validates.
Expecting to read other cluster objects from CEL. There is no I/O; use params or a webhook.
Matching pods directly to catch Deployments. Enforce on the workload resource, or the error surfaces on the ReplicaSet where nobody sees it.
kubectlTips: kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicy  — what is defined in the cluster
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybinding  — and, crucially, what is actually bound and enforcing
kubectl apply -f bad-deployment.yaml --dry-run=server  — test a policy without creating anything

summary: Activates a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy: where it applies and whether violations deny, warn or just audit.
explanation:
A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is inert on its own. The binding is what turns it on, and this separation is the point of the design: one policy definition can be rolled out gradually across a cluster by adding bindings.

`spec.validationActions` decides the consequence. `Audit` records violations in the API server audit log and changes nothing. `Warn` returns a warning that kubectl prints while still accepting the object. `Deny` rejects it. The intended workflow is to bind with `Audit` first, look at what would have broken, move to `Warn`, and only then to `Deny`. Actions can be combined.

`spec.matchResources` scopes the binding. `namespaceSelector` limits it to namespaces carrying particular labels — enforce in production, warn in staging, with one policy and two bindings. `objectSelector` narrows further by the object's own labels, which is the usual way to provide an exemption path.

`spec.paramRef` supplies a configuration object matching the policy's `paramKind`, available in expressions as `params`. That is what lets a single "allowed registries" policy be parameterised per namespace rather than hardcoded. A policy with no binding enforces nothing, and a binding referencing a policy that does not exist is inert. Both states are silent, so when a policy is not working, checking that both objects exist and that the selectors actually match is the first thing to do.
whenToUse: Rolling a policy out gradually: audit, then warn, then deny
Enforcing strictly in production while only warning in development namespaces
Parameterising one policy differently per namespace or per team
Required for any ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to have effect

keyFields.description: The ValidatingAdmissionPolicy this binding activates.
Deny, Warn and/or Audit. At least one is required.
Restrict to namespaces matching these labels.
Restrict to objects matching these labels — the usual exemption mechanism.
Configuration object exposed to the policy's CEL expressions as params.

example:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits-prod
spec:
  policyName: require-resource-limits
  validationActions:
    - Deny
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        environment: production
    objectSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: policy.example.com/exempt
          operator: DoesNotExist
commonMistakes: Writing the policy but never the binding, so nothing is enforced and nothing says so.
Going straight to Deny in production without an Audit phase, and blocking legitimate deployments.
A namespaceSelector matching no namespaces — the binding exists and does nothing.
Omitting validationActions. It is required and the binding is rejected without it.
Referencing a policy name that does not exist; the binding is accepted but inert.
kubectlTips: kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicybinding -o wide  — which policies are actually live
kubectl apply -f test.yaml --dry-run=server  — see the Deny or Warn result without creating anything
kubectl label ns staging environment=staging  — the selector target that scopes a binding

summary: Built-in enforcement of Pod security standards, configured with labels on a Namespace rather than its own object.
explanation:
**Conceptual entry — there is no PodSecurityAdmission object.** Pod Security Admission is an admission controller enabled by default since Kubernetes 1.25, and it is configured entirely through labels on Namespaces. It replaced PodSecurityPolicy, which was removed in 1.25.

It enforces three predefined Pod Security Standards. `privileged` is unrestricted. `baseline` blocks the well-known escapes — privileged containers, host namespaces, hostPath volumes, dangerous capabilities. `restricted` additionally requires running as non-root, dropping all capabilities, a seccomp profile, and no privilege escalation. Unlike PodSecurityPolicy, these levels are fixed: you pick one, you do not author your own.

The label is `pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>: <level>`, where mode is `enforce`, `audit` or `warn`. `enforce` rejects violating Pods; `audit` records them in the audit log; `warn` returns a message to the user but admits the Pod. All three can be set at once, which is exactly how you migrate: set `warn` and `audit` to `restricted` first, see what complains, then turn on `enforce`. A `<mode>-version` label pins to a specific standard version so a cluster upgrade cannot silently tighten the rules.

One behaviour catches people out. Enforcement happens on Pod creation, so a Deployment whose template violates the policy is accepted — the Deployment object is fine — and the failure occurs when its ReplicaSet tries to create Pods. Look at the ReplicaSet's events, not the Deployment's. The `warn` mode exists partly to solve this: it fires when you create the Deployment, where you will actually see it. PSA covers Pod-level security settings only. Image provenance, resource limits and naming conventions are outside its scope, which is where ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or a policy engine such as Kyverno comes in.
whenToUse: Establishing a security baseline for every namespace in a cluster
Migrating from the removed PodSecurityPolicy
Blocking privileged containers and host mounts in application namespaces
Combine with a policy engine for rules it does not cover

keyFields.description: privileged, baseline or restricted. Violating Pods are rejected.
Level recorded in the audit log without blocking.
Level that returns a warning to the client — fires on Deployment creation, where you see it.
Pin to a Kubernetes version, e.g. v1.31, so upgrades do not tighten rules silently.
Where the Pod complies: runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile, and per-container allowPrivilegeEscalation and capabilities.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: secure-apps
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.31
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: compliant-app
  namespace: secure-apps
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 50m
          memory: 64Mi
      volumeMounts:
        - name: cache
          mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
    - name: cache
      emptyDir: {}
commonMistakes: Enabling enforce: restricted on an existing namespace without warning first, and breaking every workload at once.
Looking for the rejection on the Deployment. It happens when the ReplicaSet creates Pods — check the ReplicaSet's events.
Looking for a PodSecurityPolicy object. It was removed in Kubernetes 1.25.
Omitting the version label, so a cluster upgrade can tighten the standard under you.
Assuming restricted covers everything. It says nothing about images, resource limits or network access.
kubectlTips: kubectl label ns secure-apps pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted  — see what would break, without blocking anything
kubectl get ns -L pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce  — the enforcement level of every namespace in one column
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml --dry-run=server  — get the exact violation list before creating anything

summary: Adds a brand-new resource type to the Kubernetes API, which then behaves like any built-in kind.
explanation:
A CustomResourceDefinition teaches the API server about a kind it did not previously know. Apply one for `Database` and you immediately get `kubectl get databases`, RBAC rules that can reference `databases`, label selectors, watches, and etcd storage — all the machinery of a built-in type, with no server code written. What you do not get is behaviour. A CRD only defines and stores objects. Creating a `Database` resource stores a document; it does not create a database. Something has to watch those objects and act, and that something is a controller — which is what turns a CRD into an operator.

In `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` a structural OpenAPI v3 schema is required for every version. This is not paperwork: the schema drives validation, defaulting, and pruning. Pruning matters especially — any field not described in the schema is silently stripped on write. A field that vanishes after `kubectl apply` is almost always a schema that does not declare it.

A CRD may serve several versions at once. Exactly one has `storage: true` and is what is persisted; the others are converted on read, either by `strategy: None` (identical schemas, just relabelled) or by a conversion webhook. `served: false` retires a version without deleting stored data.

Two optional pieces make custom resources feel native. `subresources.status` splits status from spec so a controller can update status without touching the user's spec, and `subresources.scale` makes `kubectl scale` and HorizontalPodAutoscaler work against your kind. `additionalPrinterColumns` controls what `kubectl get` shows, which is the difference between a useful CLI experience and a column of names. Deleting a CRD deletes every custom resource of that kind, cluster-wide and irreversibly.
whenToUse: Building an operator that manages an application with its own domain objects
Extending the cluster's vocabulary for platform teams: Environment, Tenant, Database
Configuration objects for a controller you are writing
Not for arbitrary data storage — etcd is not a database and objects are size-limited

keyFields.description: Must be exactly <plural>.<group>, e.g. databases.example.com.
API group, conventionally a domain you control.
Namespaced or Cluster.
plural, singular, kind, listKind and optional shortNames used by kubectl.
Exactly one version must be true — the one persisted to etcd.
Whether this version is exposed by the API. Set false to retire it.
Required structural schema. Undeclared fields are pruned on write.
Enables a separate status endpoint so controllers do not overwrite spec.
Makes kubectl scale and HPA work on the custom resource.
Extra columns in kubectl get output.
None or Webhook, for converting between served versions.

example:
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.example.com
spec:
  group: example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: databases
    singular: database
    kind: Database
    listKind: DatabaseList
    shortNames:
      - db
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources:
        status: {}
      additionalPrinterColumns:
        - name: Engine
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.engine
        - name: Size
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.size
        - name: Phase
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.phase
        - name: Age
          type: date
          jsonPath: .metadata.creationTimestamp
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required:
                - engine
              properties:
                engine:
                  type: string
                  enum: ["postgres", "mysql"]
                version:
                  type: string
                  default: "16"
                size:
                  type: string
                  pattern: "^[0-9]+Gi$"
                  default: "10Gi"
                replicas:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 1
                  maximum: 5
                  default: 1
            status:
              type: object
              properties:
                phase:
                  type: string
                observedGeneration:
                  type: integer
commonMistakes: Naming the CRD anything other than <plural>.<group>. The API server rejects it.
Omitting a field from the schema and watching it disappear on apply. Undeclared fields are pruned, silently.
Marking more than one version as storage: true, or none at all. Exactly one is required.
Deleting a CRD to 'clean up', taking every custom resource of that kind with it.
Forgetting subresources.status, so a controller writing status also clobbers the user's spec.
Using a group you do not own, such as k8s.io, and colliding with a future upstream API.
kubectlTips: kubectl get crd  — everything installed, which is a good map of what operators are running
kubectl explain database.spec  — works on custom resources too, generated from the schema
kubectl api-resources --api-group=example.com  — confirm the kind registered
kubectl get crd databases.example.com -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[*].name}'  — which versions are served

summary: Registers an external HTTPS service that the API server calls to approve or reject objects before they are stored.
explanation:
A validating webhook is a veto. When a matching request arrives, the API server pauses it, POSTs an `AdmissionReview` to your service, and waits for a response saying `allowed: true` or `false` with a message. Only then does the request continue. Validating webhooks run after mutating ones, so they see the final form of the object.

The webhook must be HTTPS, and the API server must trust its certificate — hence `clientConfig.caBundle`, which in practice is injected by cert-manager rather than pasted in by hand. The service normally runs in the cluster and is referenced by name and namespace. Two fields are required and easy to forget. `sideEffects` declares whether the webhook changes anything outside the request (it should be `None`, so dry-run works). `admissionReviewVersions` lists the API versions your server understands, normally `["v1"]`. Omitting either makes the manifest invalid.

`failurePolicy` is the field with the most operational consequence. `Fail` means an unreachable webhook blocks every matching request — and if your webhook matches broadly and its own Pods cannot start, you have a cluster that cannot deploy anything, including the fix. The standard defences are a `namespaceSelector` excluding `kube-system` and the webhook's own namespace, a short `timeoutSeconds`, and narrow `rules`.

Since the arrival of ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, webhooks are no longer the default answer. Reach for a webhook when the logic needs to read other objects, call an external service, or use a real programming language; use a CEL policy when it does not.
whenToUse: Validation that must consult other cluster objects or an external service
Complex rules beyond what CEL can express
Policy engines such as OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno, which install one of these
Prefer ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for simple in-object rules — no server to run or keep up

keyFields.description: Must be a fully qualified domain name with at least three segments, e.g. validate.example.com.
In-cluster Service to call, with name, namespace, path and port.
Base64 CA bundle for the webhook's certificate. Usually injected by cert-manager.
Which operations, API groups, versions and resources trigger the call.
Fail (default) or Ignore when the webhook is unreachable. Fail can wedge a cluster.
Required. None, NoneOnDryRun, Some or Unknown.
Required. AdmissionReview versions the server accepts, normally ["v1"].
Exclude system namespaces here to avoid locking yourself out.
1 to 30, default 10. Keep it low — every matching request waits this long in the worst case.
CEL preconditions evaluated in the API server before the call is made at all.

example:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: policy-validator
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/inject-ca-from: policy-system/policy-webhook-cert
webhooks:
  - name: validate.policy.example.com
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    sideEffects: None
    failurePolicy: Fail
    timeoutSeconds: 5
    matchPolicy: Equivalent
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: policy-webhook
        namespace: policy-system
        path: /validate
        port: 443
    rules:
      - operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
        scope: "Namespaced"
    namespaceSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
          operator: NotIn
          values: ["kube-system", "policy-system"]
commonMistakes: failurePolicy: Fail with a selector that includes the webhook's own namespace. If the webhook Pods go down they cannot be restarted, and the cluster cannot deploy anything.
Omitting sideEffects or admissionReviewVersions. Both are required in v1 and the object is rejected.
A webhook name with fewer than three dot-separated segments; the API server rejects it.
Forgetting to exclude kube-system, so a broken webhook blocks control-plane components.
A long timeoutSeconds, adding latency to every matching API request cluster-wide.
Using a webhook for a rule that a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy could express with no server at all.
kubectlTips: kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations  — the first thing to check when applies start failing mysteriously
kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration <name>  — the emergency escape when a Fail-policy webhook has wedged the cluster
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration <name> -o jsonpath='{.webhooks[*].failurePolicy}'  — audit the risky ones

summary: Registers an external service that can modify objects on their way into the cluster, before they are stored.
explanation:
A mutating webhook rewrites objects in flight. The API server sends the incoming object to your service, which replies with a JSON Patch, and the patched object continues through admission. This is how sidecar injection works: you apply a Deployment with one container, and the stored Pod has two.

Ordering is fixed and important. Mutating webhooks run first, then object schema validation, then validating webhooks. So a validating webhook always sees the final object, including everything the mutators added — which is why sidecars injected by a mutating webhook must themselves satisfy your validation policies.

Mutating webhooks run in sequence rather than in parallel, each seeing the previous one's output, which makes the result order-dependent and occasionally surprising. `reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded` asks the API server to call the webhook a second time if a later webhook changed the object, so a mutator can react to its peers. That means your webhook must be idempotent: a sidecar injector that does not check whether it already injected will happily inject twice.

Everything said about validating webhooks applies here too — required `sideEffects` and `admissionReviewVersions`, TLS with a `caBundle`, and the `failurePolicy: Fail` hazard of an unreachable webhook blocking the cluster. Mutating webhooks carry extra risk because they change what users asked for: someone applies a manifest, gets something different back, and nothing in their YAML explains why.
whenToUse: Service mesh sidecar injection (Istio, Linkerd)
Injecting secrets, environment variables or volumes from an external vault
Applying organisation-wide defaults such as node selectors or tolerations
Prefer a plain default in the manifest, or a LimitRange, when either would do

keyFields.description: Fully qualified name with at least three dot-separated segments.
Service reference or URL, plus the caBundle to verify its certificate.
Operations, groups, versions and resources that trigger the call.
Never (default) or IfNeeded, which may call the webhook again after other mutations.
Fail (default) or Ignore when unreachable.
Required. Use None so server-side dry-run behaves correctly.
Required, normally ["v1"].
Label-based opt-in, the usual way to make injection explicit rather than automatic.

example:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: sidecar-injector
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/inject-ca-from: mesh-system/sidecar-injector-cert
webhooks:
  - name: inject.mesh.example.com
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    sideEffects: None
    failurePolicy: Ignore
    timeoutSeconds: 5
    reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: sidecar-injector
        namespace: mesh-system
        path: /mutate
        port: 443
    rules:
      - operations: ["CREATE"]
        apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        resources: ["pods"]
        scope: "Namespaced"
    objectSelector:
      matchLabels:
        mesh-injection: enabled
    namespaceSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
          operator: NotIn
          values: ["kube-system", "mesh-system"]
commonMistakes: A non-idempotent mutator that injects a sidecar twice when reinvoked.
failurePolicy: Fail on a webhook matching all Pods — if it goes down, no Pod anywhere can be created, including its own.
Expecting a validating webhook to run before mutation. Mutation always comes first.
Mutating without an objectSelector or namespaceSelector opt-in, so users get changes they never asked for and cannot explain.
Debugging by reading the applied YAML. Use kubectl get -o yaml on the stored object to see what the mutation actually produced.
kubectlTips: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations  — what is rewriting your objects
kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml  — compare the stored object against your manifest to see the injected changes
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml --dry-run=server -o yaml  — preview mutations without creating anything

summary: A design pattern, not an API object: a custom resource plus a controller that acts on it.
explanation:
**Conceptual entry — there is no Operator kind in Kubernetes.** An operator is a pattern: a CustomResourceDefinition that describes a desired state, plus a controller (an ordinary Deployment) that watches those objects and makes reality match. The name comes from the idea of encoding a human operator's runbook in software.

The controller runs a reconciliation loop. It watches its custom resources and the objects it owns, and on every change it compares desired state to actual state and takes whatever action closes the gap — create a StatefulSet, run a backup Job, trigger a failover. Reconciliation is level-triggered, not edge-triggered: the loop is given the current state and asked to fix it, rather than a list of events to replay. That is why it is robust to missed events, restarts and duplicate notifications, and it is why reconcile functions must be idempotent — running one twice must be harmless.

Ownership is expressed through `metadata.ownerReferences` on created objects. That gives cascading deletion for free: delete the custom resource and Kubernetes garbage-collects everything it owned. Cleanup that must happen *before* deletion — deregistering from an external system, taking a final backup — uses a finalizer, a string on the object that blocks deletion until the controller removes it. A forgotten finalizer is the usual cause of an object that will not delete.

Status reporting follows a convention: the controller writes `status.conditions` and `status.observedGeneration`. Comparing `observedGeneration` to `metadata.generation` tells you whether the controller has caught up with the latest spec change. Operators are usually built with a framework — Kubebuilder or controller-runtime in Go, Operator SDK, or Kopf in Python — and are packaged with their CRDs, RBAC and Deployment together.
whenToUse: Automating stateful applications with real operational complexity: databases, message brokers
Encoding runbook knowledge — backups, failover, version upgrades — as software
Building a platform API that abstracts Kubernetes detail from application teams
Not for simple deployments; a Helm chart or plain manifests are usually enough

keyFields.description: The desired state the user declares. Defined by your CRD's schema.
Standard condition list the controller writes: type, status, reason, message.
The metadata.generation the controller has processed. Lagging behind means it has not caught up.
Links children to the custom resource so garbage collection cascades.
Blocks deletion until the controller finishes external cleanup and removes the entry.

example:
apiVersion: example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: production
spec:
  engine: postgres
  version: "16"
  size: 100Gi
  replicas: 3
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: database-operator
  namespace: operators
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database-operator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: database-operator
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: database-operator
      containers:
        - name: manager
          image: example.com/database-operator:v1.2.0
          args:
            - --leader-elect
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:
              memory: 256Mi
commonMistakes: Writing a reconcile loop that is not idempotent. It will be called repeatedly with the same state and must not duplicate work.
Adding a finalizer without a code path that removes it, leaving objects that can never be deleted.
Treating reconciliation as event handling. You get current state, not a reliable event stream — never assume you saw every change.
Omitting ownerReferences, so deleting the custom resource orphans everything it created.
Running multiple replicas without leader election, so several controllers fight over the same objects.
Granting the operator's ServiceAccount cluster-admin instead of the specific permissions it needs.
kubectlTips: kubectl get crd  — a good inventory of which operators are installed
kubectl logs deploy/database-operator -n operators -f  — reconcile errors show up here, not on the custom resource
kubectl get database orders-db -o jsonpath='{.status.observedGeneration}/{.metadata.generation}'  — whether the controller has caught up
kubectl patch database orders-db -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' --type=merge  — last-resort unstick for a deletion blocked by a dead operator

summary: A short, time-limited record of something that happened to an object — the first place to look when something is wrong.
explanation:
Events are how the control plane explains itself. The scheduler records why a Pod could not be placed, the kubelet records image pulls and probe failures, controllers record what they created. When a Pod is stuck in `Pending` and the spec looks fine, the Event says `0/5 nodes are available: insufficient cpu` — and that is the answer.

Each Event points at an object through `involvedObject` and carries a machine-readable `reason` (`FailedScheduling`, `BackOff`, `Unhealthy`), a human `message`, and a `type` of `Normal` or `Warning`. Repeated identical events are aggregated: rather than thousands of objects, one Event's `count` increments and `lastTimestamp` moves.

The critical operational fact is that **Events expire**. The default retention is one hour, after which they are deleted from etcd. They are diagnostic breadcrumbs, not an audit log — if you need history, ship them to a logging system, and use the audit log for compliance.

There are two APIs over the same data. Core `v1` Event is the original and what `kubectl get events` returns by default; `events.k8s.io/v1` is a newer, better-structured version of the same information, with `note` in place of `message` and clearer reporting fields. Both are current and served. One persistent annoyance: `kubectl get events` sorts by name, which is effectively random. Always sort explicitly by timestamp, or the output is nearly useless.
whenToUse: Diagnosing a Pod stuck Pending, CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff
Finding out why an eviction, preemption or rollout happened
Seeing quota rejections, which surface on the ReplicaSet rather than the Deployment
Not for long-term history — they are deleted after about an hour

keyFields.description: The object this event is about: kind, name, namespace and uid.
Short CamelCase code such as FailedScheduling, Unhealthy or BackOff. The best thing to filter on.
Human-readable detail — usually the actual answer to what went wrong.
Normal or Warning.
How many times this event has repeated since firstTimestamp.
Most recent occurrence. Sort by this, never by name.
Which component reported it — kubelet, default-scheduler, a controller.

example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Event
metadata:
  name: web-5d8f9c7b6d-x2k9p.17a3b4c5d6e7f890
  namespace: default
involvedObject:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  name: web-5d8f9c7b6d-x2k9p
  namespace: default
reason: FailedScheduling
message: "0/5 nodes are available: 5 Insufficient cpu."
type: Warning
reportingComponent: default-scheduler
reportingInstance: default-scheduler
source:
  component: default-scheduler
firstTimestamp: "2026-01-15T10:00:00Z"
lastTimestamp: "2026-01-15T10:04:00Z"
count: 5
commonMistakes: Expecting events to still be there tomorrow. Default retention is one hour.
Running kubectl get events without sorting. The default order is by name and tells you nothing.
Looking only at the Pod's events for a Deployment problem. Quota and admission failures land on the ReplicaSet.
Treating events as an audit trail. They are best-effort and can be dropped under load; use the audit log for compliance.
Missing that an event repeated 500 times, because the count field is easy to overlook in wide output.
kubectlTips: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp  — the one form worth memorising
kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning  — skip the noise
kubectl describe pod <name>  — the Events section at the bottom, already filtered to that object
kubectl get events -A --watch  — follow cluster activity live during a rollout
kubectl events --for pod/web-abc -n default  — the newer dedicated subcommand

summary: Live CPU and memory usage per container, served by metrics-server and consumed by kubectl top and the HPA.
explanation:
**Not part of the core API server, and read-only.** PodMetrics is served by metrics-server, an add-on that registers itself through an APIService for the `metrics.k8s.io` group. On a cluster without it, `kubectl top pods` fails and every HPA reports `<unknown>`. The example below shows what the API returns; there is nothing to apply.

metrics-server scrapes the kubelet's summary API on every node roughly every 15 seconds and keeps the results in memory only. Nothing is written to etcd and nothing is retained — you can ask what CPU a Pod is using now, but not what it was using an hour ago. That is a deliberate design decision: this is the resource metrics pipeline for autoscaling, not a monitoring system. For history you want Prometheus or an equivalent.

The values are `cpu` in nanocores-derived quantities (`250m` means a quarter of a core) and `memory` as a byte quantity, usually the container's working set. Working set is not the same as RSS, and it is what the kubelet uses for eviction decisions — so it is the number that matters when a container is being OOM-killed.

This is also where the gap between requests and reality is visible. The scheduler packs nodes by requests; `kubectl top` shows what is actually consumed. Comparing the two across a cluster is usually the fastest way to find how much capacity is being reserved and wasted. The API has been at `v1beta1` for years and is stable in practice despite the name.
whenToUse: kubectl top pods — checking what a workload actually consumes
Powering HorizontalPodAutoscaler CPU and memory targets
Rightsizing requests by comparing usage against what is reserved
Not for dashboards, alerting or history — use Prometheus

keyFields.description: Container the sample belongs to.
CPU usage as a quantity, e.g. 250m for a quarter core.
Working-set memory, the figure the kubelet uses for eviction.
When the sample was taken.
Interval the sample covers, typically around 30 seconds.

example:
# Read-only: served by metrics-server. This is API output, not a manifest.
apiVersion: metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: PodMetrics
metadata:
  name: web-5d8f9c7b6d-x2k9p
  namespace: default
timestamp: "2026-01-15T10:05:00Z"
window: 30s
containers:
  - name: nginx
    usage:
      cpu: 250m
      memory: 128Mi
  - name: sidecar
    usage:
      cpu: 15m
      memory: 32Mi
commonMistakes: Expecting it to work without metrics-server installed. It is an add-on, not part of the API server.
Trying to query historical usage. Metrics are in-memory and current only.
Confusing usage with requests. The scheduler uses requests; this shows actual consumption.
Alerting on these values. There is no retention and no alerting — use Prometheus.
Assuming memory here is RSS. It is working set, which includes some page cache and is what drives eviction.
kubectlTips: kubectl top pods --containers  — per-container breakdown rather than Pod totals
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory  — find the heaviest workloads in the cluster
kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/pods | jq  — the raw API behind kubectl top
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io  — check this first when kubectl top fails

summary: Live CPU and memory usage per node, served by metrics-server and shown by kubectl top nodes.
explanation:
**Not part of the core API server, and read-only.** NodeMetrics is the node-level counterpart to PodMetrics, served by the same metrics-server through the same aggregated APIService. The example below is API output rather than a manifest.

It answers a question the Node object cannot: how busy is this machine *right now*. The Node's `status.allocatable` and the sum of Pod requests tell you what the scheduler has committed; NodeMetrics tells you what is actually being used. Those two numbers routinely differ by a large factor, and that gap is where cluster cost hides.

The practical use is diagnosing the two opposite failures. A node whose requests are exhausted but whose usage is low means Pods are over-requesting, and the fix is smaller requests, not more nodes. A node whose usage is near capacity while requests look modest means Pods are under-requesting and are heading for CPU throttling or OOM kills — the fix is larger requests, and possibly limits.

`kubectl top nodes` shows both the absolute usage and the percentage, where the percentage is against the node's `allocatable`, not its total capacity. Allocatable excludes what the kubelet and system daemons have reserved, so it is always somewhat lower than the machine's nominal size. As with PodMetrics, values are current-only and held in memory.
whenToUse: kubectl top nodes — a quick read on real cluster utilisation
Deciding whether the cluster is genuinely full or merely over-requested
Investigating node pressure, throttling or OOM kills
Not for capacity planning over time — use a monitoring system with retention

keyFields.description: Current CPU usage for the whole node as a quantity.
Current working-set memory for the whole node.
When the sample was taken.
Interval the sample covers.

example:
# Read-only: served by metrics-server. This is API output, not a manifest.
apiVersion: metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: NodeMetrics
metadata:
  name: node-1
timestamp: "2026-01-15T10:05:00Z"
window: 30s
usage:
  cpu: 1250m
  memory: 6Gi
commonMistakes: Comparing usage against total machine capacity. kubectl top reports against allocatable, which is smaller.
Adding nodes because the scheduler says the cluster is full, when actual usage shows Pods are over-requesting.
Expecting a history of node load. There is none — metrics are in-memory and current only.
Assuming an empty result means the nodes are idle. It usually means metrics-server is not running.
kubectlTips: kubectl top nodes  — usage and percentage of allocatable per node
kubectl describe node <name> | grep -A5 'Allocated resources'  — requests, to compare against actual usage
kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes | jq  — the raw data behind the command

summary: Tells Prometheus which Services to scrape metrics from, declaratively instead of by editing config files.
explanation:
**Not part of Kubernetes.** ServiceMonitor is a CustomResourceDefinition from the Prometheus Operator, the de-facto standard way Prometheus is run on Kubernetes (and what the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart installs). Without that operator, the kind does not exist.

It is included here because monitoring is a genuine gap in core Kubernetes. The metrics-server pipeline exists purely to feed autoscaling; there is no built-in object for "scrape this application's metrics". ServiceMonitor fills that gap in a way that fits Kubernetes conventions.

The mechanism is a chain of label selectors. A ServiceMonitor selects Services by label; the operator resolves those Services to their EndpointSlices and generates Prometheus scrape configuration targeting the individual Pods. Meanwhile the Prometheus custom resource has its own `serviceMonitorSelector` choosing which ServiceMonitors to honour. Both links must match, and a ServiceMonitor that the Prometheus instance does not select is silently ignored — the single most common reason a target never appears.

`spec.endpoints[].port` refers to the **name** of a port on the Service, not a number. An unnamed Service port cannot be scraped this way, which is why metrics ports are conventionally named `metrics`. By default a ServiceMonitor only matches Services in its own namespace; `namespaceSelector` widens that, with `any: true` meaning cluster-wide. PodMonitor is the sibling object for scraping Pods that have no Service in front of them, and PrometheusRule holds alerting and recording rules in the same declarative style.
whenToUse: Adding an application's /metrics endpoint to Prometheus on a cluster running the Prometheus Operator
Keeping scrape configuration next to the application it belongs to, in Git
Scraping exporters such as node-exporter or kube-state-metrics
Use PodMonitor instead when there is no Service in front of the Pods

keyFields.description: Labels identifying the Services to scrape.
Which namespaces to look in. Defaults to the ServiceMonitor's own; any: true means all.
The Service port's name — not a number. The port must be named.
Metrics path, default /metrics.
Scrape interval, e.g. 30s.
http or https.
Prometheus relabeling rules applied before the scrape.
Must match the Prometheus resource's serviceMonitorSelector, or this object is ignored.

example:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: production
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
      - production
  endpoints:
    - port: metrics
      path: /metrics
      interval: 30s
      scheme: http
commonMistakes: Expecting it to work without the Prometheus Operator installed. It is a CRD, not a Kubernetes API.
Labels that do not match the Prometheus instance's serviceMonitorSelector, so the object is ignored with no error anywhere.
Using a port number in spec.endpoints[].port. It must be the Service port's name.
An unnamed metrics port on the Service, which cannot be selected at all.
Forgetting namespaceSelector when the Service is in a different namespace from the ServiceMonitor.
kubectlTips: kubectl get servicemonitor -A  — every scrape configuration in the cluster
kubectl get prometheus -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.serviceMonitorSelector}'  — the selector your labels must satisfy
kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus-operated 9090 -n monitoring  — then check Status > Targets in the UI to see whether the scrape landed
